At least three civilians were killed in a Russian attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk, regional authorities said on Tuesday.

Two other people were injured in the attack, the Donetsk regional prosecutor's office said on social media.

Three housing blocks were damaged by shelling, the authorities said.

Investigators are still working to determine what type of weapon was used.

The industrial city of Kramatorsk lies around 15 kilometres from the front line and is part of a network of heavily fortified cities defending the last remaining Ukrainian-held areas of the Donetsk region.

Ukraine has been defending itself against Russia's full-scale invasion since February 2022.

https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ck9qzn.heading: Zelensky prepares for Oslo talks with US envoys as Rubio denies withholding intelligence
https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ck9qzn.body:
US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with Volodymyr Zelensky with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the meeting with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine".

Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected as "scandalous" and "outrageous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv.

He was speaking after Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, told the BBC that the lack of reliable US warnings meant lives were being lost.

"This looks very strange," said Beskrestnov. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."

Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Støre said the aim of the Oslo talks were to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace.

Zelensky said earlier he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network.

Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to the Starlink network in Ukraine, and unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors had not yet been approved.

The US secretary of state is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.

Witkoff is expected to be joined by video-link by Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, and by several European representatives, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and officials from the UK, Poland, France and Germany, as well as the EU and Nato.

It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia after his visit to Oslo, however the Kremlin spokesman said he hoped a meeting with Trump's special envoy could be organised in the near future. Dmitry Peskov said "we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators".

Earlier this month Russia's Vladimir Putin discussed the war with Trump over the phone, and afterwards the US president announced that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

Trump's deal with the Russian leader coincided with Witkoff and Kushner's last meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami, and Zelensky reacted by calling it "a happy birthday present for Putin".

Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have reached record highs at the pump since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke on Monday of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".

He pointed out that the US had not been paying for the defence of Ukraine since the start of 2025, and Europe and other countries were shouldering the burden.

"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.

Asked whether or not Ukraine was a US ally, Vice-President JD Vance has said in a TV interview that Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".

"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too."

"I think the important takeaway is that there has ​not been some deliberate political directive to go ⁠out and harm Ukraine," he told journalists as he kicked ​off his India trip.

"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," ​Rubio said.

Rubio added that he had had a 45-minute conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on Tuesday. Zelenskiy said the topics included ballistic ​missile interceptors, early warning of Russian attacks and the ​situation with Starlink and Starshield satellite services, which the Ukrainian president said ‌needed ⁠to be restored.

The comments come as Reuters earlier reported that US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had yet to authorize delivery of the latest package of US weaponry purchased by NATO ​allies under PURL.

Zelenskiy ​had also ⁠said the Pentagon has delayed the delivery of missiles under the programme, as relations between Kyiv ​and Washington have deteriorated this month as US ​President ⁠Donald Trump courted Moscow.

Israel and Lebanon will hold US-mediated discussions at the “working level” in Tampa, Florida, today, without the participation of Jerusalem’s or Beirut’s ambassador to Washington, a US official tells The Times of Israel.

The talks set for October 20-21 are expected to focus on advancing the Trilateral Framework Agreement aimed at disarming Hezbollah and the gradual withdrawal of Israeli troops from southern Lebanon.

Lebanon’s presidency said last week that its military delegation will demand an end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon at the trilateral meeting.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told The Times of Israel during a briefing on Sunday that Israel would demand that the Lebanese Armed Forces demonstrate its ability to clear Hezbollah threats from two designated pilot areas under the framework, warning that Israel would take action itself if the Lebanese military failed to do so.

“We gave you two ‘pilot zones’ – go in, clear them out. Can you do it? Good. You can’t do it? We’ll take care of it,” he said.

He also suggested that Hezbollah’s elimination could pave the way for peace between Israel and Lebanon, but did not specify a deadline for the Lebanese military to disarm the terror group.

The talks come amid heightened tensions within Lebanon over communications between the two countries, including a legal complaint filed against Lebanese Ambassador to the US Nada Hamadeh Moawad after she allegedly contacted Israeli ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter to condemn the West Bank car ramming attack that left his son in critical condition — in apparent violation of Lebanon’s laws forbidding direct contact with Israel. The US State Department publicly condemned the complaint against Moawad and was weighing sanctions against Lebanese judges involved in handling it, a US official familiar with the matter told The Times of Israel last week.

https://www.rudaw.net/english/categories.body: ERBIL, Kurdistan Region - Iran’s maritime authority has blacklisted 122 commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, with 40 facing “enforcement action” amid an escalating standoff with Washington over control of the strategic waterway, as Tehran officials warn escalation could trigger a global energy crisis. "122 vessels have been added to the Persian Gulf Waterway Non-Compliance List," the Persian Gulf Strait Authority announced in a statement published by Fars News Agency, affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), early Tuesday, adding that “enforcement action has been taken against more than 40 vessels” The Authority noted that 19 vessels are currently negotiating to prevent inclusion on the non-compliance list, two vessels have agreed to fulfil their obligations to be delisted, and approximately 30 vessels will be added to the list if they fail to respond to warnings. The announcement comes amid a sharp escalation in attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway connecting the Persian Gulf to international shipping routes. At least 26 attacks have been carried out on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters as of Sunday, the highest monthly tally since the second Iran war began on February 28, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute. The attacks have intensified as Iran and the United States compete for control of the strategic passage following the outbreak of war between Tehran, Washington, and Tel Aviv in late February. Several vessels have been struck by missiles, drones, and other projectiles in recent weeks, with some attacks causing fires, casualties, and significant damage in the energy corridor. On Monday, IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi stated that Tehran does not rule out the possibility of war, warning that any Iranian response will be "much more severe." Mohebbi added that the United States will face massive troubles in the event of an escalation and that the "world will suffer a serious energy crisis." Highlighting the strategic vulnerability of the region, the spokesperson added, "7 major cables pass under the Strait of Hormuz, on which all the world's internet and commercial data depend; we mention this as a reminder so that the enemy knows." The US Central Command (CENTCOM) stated on Saturday that since reinstating the maritime blockade on Iranian ports, its forces had redirected 138 commercial vessels to ensure compliance. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/alba.heading: Albania's PM Edi Rama blames 'hybrid war' for fuelling unrest across the country | Euronews
https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/alba.body:
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama blamed a "hybrid war" for fuelling unrest in his country on Tuesday, after a week of violent anti-government demonstrations in the capital Tirana.

Demonstrators have repeatedly clashed with police since Tuesday as months of protests escalate, driven by fresh demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and renewed calls for Rama's resignation.

During the demonstrations, which have drawn thousands, police have regularly used water cannon, tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse crowds that have targeted government buildings and smashed stores in several parts of the capital.

Protesters have hurled stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at police.

Around 300 people have been injured in the clashes, more than half of them police, according to authorities.

On Tuesday, Rama repeated earlier accusations that "foreign actors" were to blame for the violence, previously accusing both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation.

"This has now been recognised and is becoming a major issue across Europe," he said in a statement broadcast live while visiting the education ministry.

"It is a hybrid war that gains traction precisely because it is rooted in genuine grievances, not mere fantasy," the prime minister added, citing the rising cost of living, housing affordability and concerns for the future.

He also hinted at a possible ban on social media for children under 16 and flagged changes to the age of criminal responsibility.

Since protests began, high school students have also attended protests alongside their university counterparts, with police and authorities regularly condemning the involvement of minors in violence.

On Tuesday morning, hundreds of university professors marched in solidarity with the demonstrators to condemn police violence targeting students, according to an AFP reporter.

Carrying a banner reading "Stop violence against students", the marchers called for Rama to resign.

The week-long demonstrations have badly damaged several government buildings, including the education ministry, which remains a focal point.

The anti-government protests in the Balkan nation began over a controversial resort development in an ecologically protected area linked to US President Donald Trump's family.

But anger over the development has morphed into a broader push against corruption amid ongoing demands that Rama step down.

Albania’s Supreme Court has announced the postponement of court hearings, except for urgent cases, following property damage and damage to judicial files caused by a fire during the protests on October 17.

In a public statement issued on October 20, the court said that damage to its premises and infrastructure had disrupted normal judicial operations.

According to the Supreme Court, hearings will remain postponed until inspections of the damage are completed, the condition of judicial files is assessed, and the necessary conditions for resuming operations are restored.

The court has mobilized its staff to address the situation, with priority given to identifying and assessing damaged documents and ensuring the integrity of judicial case files.

The court said that affected parties would be notified individually using their contact details, while new hearing dates would be published on its official website and through other communication channels.

The Supreme Court has called for understanding from litigants and their legal representatives, emphasizing that restoring normal operations will require time and careful attention to ensure that judicial proceedings can resume safely.

https://english.gazetatema.net/kosovo-re.body:
Two new laws address Croatian objections that could hold up Montenegro's bid to join the European Union.

PODGORICA, 20 October 2026 — Montenegro has passed two laws aimed at settling disputes with Croatia that could delay its membership of the European Union.

The first protects historical memorials, including a plaque commemorating Croatian prisoners held at the Morinj detention camp during the wars of the 1990s.

The second prevents sports facilities from being named after people who died less than 40 years ago. It could require a swimming pool in Kotor to drop the name of Zoran Gopcevic, whom Croatia accuses of serving as a guard commander at Morinj.

The disputes are among eight issues Croatia wants resolved before Montenegro joins the EU. They include wartime disappearances, compensation claims and border disagreements.

Croatia, as an EU member, can block Montenegro's accession.

The two laws address some of Zagreb's demands, but the remaining disputes have yet to be settled.

https://europeanwesternbalkans.com/2026/.body:
PODGORICA – Montenegro’s parliament has backed a proposal to introduce mandatory integrity checks for nominees for prime minister and cabinet posts, in a vote linked by the government to the country’s EU accession commitments. The proposal received the support of 56MPs, exceeding the required two-thirds majority.

The vote does not complete the constitutional amendment process. Parliament instructed its Constitutional Committee to prepare draft amendments within four days and submit them to MPs.

According to Radio Television of Montenegro (RTCG) the proposed changes would prevent anyone who fails to meet integrity requirements prescribed by law from being nominated to lead or join the government. They aim to strengthen accountability and prevent corruption and conflicts of interest.

MPs also supported a provision requiring the legislation governing these checks to be adopted by a two-thirds parliamentary majority.

The Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS), the URA Civic Movement and the Democratic People’s Party (DNP) withheld support.

DPS leader Danijel Živković argued that the mechanism could undermine voters’ choices and questioned why checks would cover government nominees but exclude other senior officials. DNP opposed the changes because they did not address its demand to make Serbian an official language.

Deputy Prime Minister Momo Koprivica defended the proposal as a safeguard for democratic institutions and described it as a prerequisite for closing Chapter 23, which covers judiciary and fundamental rights in EU accession negotiations.

Reacting on X, Prime Minister Milojko Spajić said the vote had revealed which parties genuinely wanted Montenegro in the EU and which were prepared to obstruct its European path in pursuit of others’ interests.

https://english.republika.mk/macedonia/f.body:
A representative from the Embassy of the Republic of Bulgaria—serving as Chargé d’Affaires in the absence of Ambassador Zhelyazko Radukov—was summoned today to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. During the meeting, as reported by the Ministry, dissatisfaction was expressed regarding a recent statement by the Minister of Interior of the Republic of Bulgaria, Ivan Demerdzhiev, concerning the case of Iva Mihajlova; the statement was characterized as offensive and provocative.

The Ministry also expressed dissatisfaction with a statement made by Ambassador Radukov to the Bulgarian television channel bTV, viewing it as direct interference in the country’s internal affairs, given the characterizations made regarding the work of the competent institutions. It was specifically emphasized that such provocations steer the bilateral dialogue away from the framework within which good-neighborly relations should develop—a framework based on mutual respect, restraint, and constructive communication, the Ministry stated.

In this context, it was noted that such conduct could necessitate an appropriate institutional response, in accordance with the provisions of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which clearly defines the scope of diplomatic activity and the principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of the receiving state. At the conclusion of the meeting, our commitment to developing good-neighborly relations—based on mutual respect, trust, and European principles—was reaffirmed; we expect a corresponding level of commitment and responsibility from the Bulgarian side, the statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade (MFAFT) noted.

Discussing the case in an interview/podcast, Ivan Demerdzhiev confirmed that Bulgaria had received an extradition request from the Macedonian authorities, but emphasized that Sofia has no intention of extraditing Mihajlova. Addressing the matter, Demerdzhiev stated that the Bulgarian police would not hand Mihajlova over to the “Serbian authorities”—referring directly to the Macedonian state authorities.

“The answer is no—we are neither seeking her nor will we hand her over to the Serbian authorities,” he said. When the journalist, Karbovski, asked if this was a slip of the tongue, Demerdzhiev admitted he had made a mistake, but added that it was “not such a big mistake.”

Meanwhile, the Bulgarian Ambassador to Macedonia, Zhelyazko Radukov, made statements that further strained diplomatic relations; the Macedonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs characterized these remarks as direct interference in the country’s internal affairs. In an interview with the Bulgarian television station bTV, Radukov stated that he “would be extremely surprised if the Macedonian authorities were unaware of Iva Mihajlova’s departure.” He openly questioned how it was possible for her to leave the country without their knowledge or some form of coordination, given the active judicial restrictions, the confiscation of her travel documents, and the police measures in place.

https://balkaninsight.com/2026/10/20/kos.heading: Kosovo Risks Losing More EU Funds After Deadlock Delayed Reforms | Balkan Insight
https://balkaninsight.com/2026/10/20/kos.body:
After nearly two years of political deadlock, Kosovo forfeited 40 million euros in EU Growth Plan funding in June and risks losing another 90 million euros, with just over two months left to implement 23 reforms.

The EU’s 6-billion-euro Growth Plan for the Western Balkans for 2024-2027 aims to accelerate the region’s integration into the EU single market and support reforms through performance-based financing.

Under the plan, Kosovo was set to receive a total of 882.6 millioneuros to support its EU accession aspirations.

The EU conditioned countries on fulfilling selected reforms under the adopted Reform Agenda and meeting conditions.

But two years on political instability in Kosovo has delayed ratification of the agreements needed to begin implementation. As a result, Pristina has received only 61.8 million euros in pre-financing. This was just 7 per cent of its total allocation.

Earlier this month, Kosovo’s squabbling parties reached a deal that many hope will put the legislature back on track after three elections in two years and a debilitating row over who should be appointed president.

But much work remains to be done, and much time has been lost in political wrangling, election campaigns and post-poll negotiations.

Kosovo’s Head of Negotiations with the EU, Jeton Zulfaj, states that all the required reforms must be implemented by the end of December, or Kosovo will forfeit more than 90 million euros.

“A total of 131.4 million euros in funding from the European Union’s Growth Plan must be allocated to this package of reforms,” Zulfaj told BIRN.

After three failed attempts, parliament narrowly passed the anti-money laundering law on Friday, one of the key laws in the reform package that would enable Kosovo to join the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA). Kosovo’s non-membership of SEPA had been costing its citizens some 55 million euros per year.

However, 16 other laws still need to be adopted by December.

“Securing the votes, especially for some of these laws, remains a challenge,” Zulfaj admitted.

Kujtim Dobruna, director of ECIKS, an NGO focused on sustainable economic development, investment promotion and public-private sector growth in Kosovo, said that losing EU funds simply due to failure to meet the criteria was irresponsible.

“For a small economy like Kosovo, more than 100 million euros is a significant amount, especially when we still face basic infrastructure problems that should have been resolved long ago,” he told BIRN. “Kosovo cannot afford this.”

Following a June deadline, Kosovo submitted its first formal disbursement request in July. In its request, Kosovo claimed progress in anti-corruption, women’s and youth employment, judicial accountability and early childhood education enrolment. But it did not explain the exact extent to which these criteria had been fulfilled.

Kosovo has requested 142.6 million euros, including 66.3 million euros for direct disbursement to the Kosovo Treasury and 76.3 million euros through the Western Balkans Investment Framework, WBIF. Of the total requested, 35.3 million euros was in loans and 40.9 million in non-repayable support.

The European Commission confirmed that the request is under assessment, with the amounts expected to be clarified by the end of October.

“Kosovo risks losing additional funds if it fails to meet a reform milestone by the end of the grace period. For 23 of the 64 milestones, originally due in 2025, that period expired at the end of June 2026,” the European Commission told BIRN.

The Commission is assessing whether Kosovo has met each requirement. “Each milestone effectively has its own price tag, and payments are released based on the level of implementation,” it noted.

In practice, the Commission enjoys broad discretion over how the funds are used and could redirect them to other priorities.

According to the Commission, implementation of the Growth Plan in the region has been highly uneven. While some countries have advanced reforms and secured EU funding, others, including Kosovo and Serbia, are making slower progress.

The €140 million already withdrawn from Kosovo and Bosnia and Herzegovina has remained in the region after being transferred to the European Innovation Council Compartment for the Western Balkans.

The next reporting deadline comes in January 2027, when the grace periods for steps originally due in 2025 expire.

According to the Commission, slow progress in implementing reforms puts Kosovo, Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina at risk of losing hundreds of millions of euros in total. All three countries have seen significant delays in adopting their reform agendas and accessing initial funding, risking permanent cuts to their allocations.

Kosovo’s Prime Minister Albin Kurti (and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen shake hands ahead of their meeting in Pristina, October 2024. Photo: EPA/VISAR KRYEZIU.

Despite robust average annual economic growth of around 4 per cent, Kosovo remains one of the poorest countries in Europe, struggling with high unemployment, a weak education system and continued emigration.

However, Kosovo’s officials insist progress on reforms is being made.

The Prime Minister’s Office said significant Reform Agendas have now been adopted. “A substantial number of milestones have already been completed, and implementation is accelerating,” it told BIRN.

About 46.5 per cent of the funds secured through reforms consists of loans provided as budget support and spent through the budget without conditions.

The remaining 53.5 per cent comprises 28.70 per cent in grants and 24.80 per cent in loans, allocated through the Western Balkans Investment Framework to finance infrastructure projects.

“Kosovo will apply for grants and loans under calls to be announced by the end of 2027,” the Office of the Coordinator for EU Reforms told BIRN.

Njomza Arifi, director of the Pristina-based Group for Legal and Political Studies, warns that the remaining time is too short to implement complex reforms requiring legislation, executive decisions and verifiable results for the EU.

“Faster decision-making and more intensive work are needed to limit further financial losses, but urgency must not compromise the quality of reforms,” she told BIRN.

To make the most of the remaining time, Arifi says the government needs a concrete action plan: “It should establish a dedicated internal mechanism to prioritize reforms.”

Kosovo continues to face serious challenges related to energy, drinking water supply, sewage and wastewater treatment, damaged riverbeds, environmental pollution, inadequate road infrastructure, and a railway system that remains stuck in the 19th century. Some of the funds were intended to cover some of these areas.

The EU Growth Plan programme is not expected to be extended beyond 2027.

“We are losing investments, reforms, and time. Both Kosovo and the EU need to ask what we have achieved with this money and what tangible improvements it has delivered,” Dobruna said.

https://www.moldpres.md/eng/society/mold.heading: Moldova's National Police to benefit from new cooperation project with Germany; initiative aims to strengthen operational, investigative capacities
https://www.moldpres.md/eng/society/mold.body:
The General Police Inspectorate (IGP) will benefit from a new cooperation project with Germany, aimed at strengthening operational and investigative capacities. The subject today was discussed by the leadership of the National Police at a meeting with a delegation from Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), led by Director Holger Münch.

The discussions focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation, developing the operational and investigative capacities of the National Police and identifying joint solutions to combat cross-border crime.

During the meeting, IGP Chief Viorel Cernauteanu praised Germany’s continued support for the modernization and development of the institution.

“It is a privilege for the National Police that you have chosen Moldova as the first destination of your regional working visit. This presence reconfirms the constant interest and commitment of German partners to the development and modernization of Moldova’s Police,” Viorel Cernauteanu said.

Over the years, the cooperation between the IGP and the BKA has contributed to the development of forensic expertise, the provision of specialized equipment to operational units and the professional training of National Police employees.

In the context of the current regional security situation, the sides addressed the main challenges faced by law enforcement authorities, as well as the need to strengthen capacities, in order to prevent and combat threats to public security.

An important moment of the meeting was the signing of a Joint Declaration of Intent on the implementation of a cooperation project between the IGP and the BKA, with the support of the Federal Government of Germany, for the period 2026–2027. The project aims to strengthen the operational, technical and investigative capacities of the police.

The parties also discussed priorities for cooperation during the next period, with a view to developing modern and effective tools to combat crime.

“We extend our sincere thanks to the Federal Government of Germany for its continued support for Moldova. Our common goal is for every citizen to feel safe, both at home and in their community,” the IGP chief noted.

The cooperation between the IGP and the BKA contributes to the development of modern and sustainable capacities compatible with European standards in the field of investigations and police cooperation. By strengthening international partnerships, the IGP reaffirms its commitment to preventing and combating crime, contributing to the safety of citizens and the security of the European space.

https://ipn.md/en/stratcom-the-falsehood.heading: StratCom: The falsehood about the secret drone factory, amplified by 13 Telegram accounts - ipn.md
https://ipn.md/en/stratcom-the-falsehood.body:
The false narrative about the secret construction of a drone factory in the Republic of Moldova was amplified in a coordinated manner by 13 Telegram accounts. According to the Center for Strategic Communication and Counter-Disinformation, on the 16th and 17th of October, these accounts posted 21 entries on this subject, without presenting evidence to support the claims, reports IPN.

According to the institution, four of the involved accounts belong to Sputnik Moldova, and the others are associated with it. Approximately three hours after the appearance of the first messages, the spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry, Maria Zaharova, described the Republic of Moldova as a Western anti-Russian testing ground.

StratCom asserts that the falsehood emerged against the backdrop of the increasing incidents involving Russian drones violating the airspace of the Republic of Moldova. Between October 10-16, seven such cases were reported.

The institution warns that the narrative about the alleged drone factory falls within the messages regarding the “militarization of the Republic of Moldova” and aims to create confusion between false information and real drone incidents. At the same time, qualifying these incidents as “hysteria” may diminish the population’s confidence in official warnings about airspace security.

The short interval between the initial messages and their amplification, the number of accounts involved, and the speed of propagation indicate, according to StratCom, more of a coordinated amplification rather than a spontaneous reaction.

https://www.moldpres.md/eng/politics/mol.body:
The Foreign Affairs Ministry (MAE) has sent a protest note to Ukraine after two border guards from the neighboring country illegally crossed the state border and entered the territory of Moldova, while attempting to detain a Ukrainian citizen. The information was confirmed by Lilian Carp, chair of the parliamentary commission for national security, defense and public order, during the „La 360 de grade” (At 360 Degrees) programme on Radio Moldova.

„The Ministry of Foreign Affairs Ministry sent a protest note regarding this, more precisely, illegal crossing. Nothing justifies such conduct by border guards, including the illegal crossing by a citizen. What the Ukrainian border guards did does not conform to any ethical standards or normal conduct. As far as I know, this incident was discussed with the Ukrainian authorities,” Lilian Carp said.

The Ukrainian citizen targeted by the detention operation has requested asylum in Moldova, and his application could be accepted if the conditions stipulated by law are met, Lilian Carp said.

„According to the legislation, he may apply for asylum on the territory of Moldova. After meeting all requirements, he will most likely be granted asylum,” Lilian Carp said.

According to the Border Police, on October 15, near the village of Holosnita, two Ukrainian border guards crossed the state border from Ukraine into Moldova during an operation to detain a Ukrainian citizen.

An event titled "The Middle Corridor and Its Prospects: The Future of Connectivity Between Azerbaijan, Korea and Eurasia" was held jointly by the Center of Analysis of International Relations (AIR Center) and the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in Azerbaijan.

The discussions focused on the Middle Corridor’s role in developing regional and international transport and logistics links, as well as opportunities to expand cooperation between Azerbaijan and South Korea. Participants also exchanged views on strengthening connectivity across Eurasia and developing trade ties.

Farid Shafiyev, Chairman of the Board of the AIR Center, said the Middle Corridor had become particularly relevant amid growing demand for stable and secure connections between Asia and Europe.

He stressed the importance of international platforms and organizations in this regard, noting that Azerbaijan had hosted the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) the previous week. Azerbaijan also maintains active ties with the European Union and other international platforms and is one of the key driving forces behind the Organization of Turkic States.

"I believe the issues to be discussed today, particularly the growth in cargo transportation through the Middle Corridor and the expansion of trade relations, demonstrate the importance of the steps being taken in this direction," Shafiyev pointed out.

South Korean Ambassador to Azerbaijan Kim Gu Kang said the event aimed to deepen understanding of the Middle Corridor’s strategic importance and explore opportunities for cooperation between South Korea and Azerbaijan.

He emphasized that developments in the South Caucasus were being closely monitored, partly because South Korea and Azerbaijan faced certain similarities in their geopolitical circumstances.

According to the ambassador, both countries have had to navigate complex regional relations. He described the initialling of the text of a peace agreement between Azerbaijan and Armenia as an important step toward lasting peace and stability in the region.

Professor Su-hong Chae, Director of the Asia Center at Seoul National University, said the Middle Corridor had significant strategic importance for developing economic and transport links between Azerbaijan and South Korea.

He added that strengthening regional peace and stability and expanding cooperation in transport, energy and digital infrastructure could create new partnership opportunities for the two countries.

Israeli media outlet Globes is reporting that Azerbaijan is the unnamed customer for $235 million worth of precision-guided missiles and rocket artillery systems from Elbit Systems. The Israeli defence company announced on 19 October that the deal for an unspecified ‘European’ customer will be fulfilled over the next three years in a move which underscores the deepening defence partnership between Baku and Tel Aviv.

At the time of publication, Elbit Systems had not yet commented on the customer but had confirmed the deal.

The Azerbaijan-Israel alliance is built on shared strategic interests: Israel gains access to energy resources, while Azerbaijan benefits from advanced military technology. This partnership proved significant during the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War in 2020, when Israeli-made long-range drones and other precision weapons helped Azerbaijani forces identify and strike Armenian positions.

According to Elbit, the agreement includes EXTRA-MR medium-range rockets, PULS launchers and logistical support, and deliveries and implementation are expected to take place over three years. The EXTRA-MR is designed for precision strikes against targets at ranges of up to 80 kilometres.

Elbit said that the agreement was signed as part of an intergovernmental arrangement between Israel’s Ministry of Defence and the customer country’s defence ministry.

The reported missile agreement comes amid renewed momentum in defence cooperation between Israel and Azerbaijan, with Israeli defence companies expanding their presence in the South Caucasus country.

Around a week earlier, Globes reported that Israeli firearms manufacturer Ari Arms had inaugurated a rifle factory in Azerbaijan in the presence of President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva.

The facility, owned by the Azerbaijani government, is expected to become the country’s first production site for Western-style M4 rifles. The plant previously focused on manufacturing Kalashnikov-style firearms.

Production of the M4 rifles is being developed through a joint venture involving Ari Arms, Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Defence Industry, headed by Minister Vugar Mustafayev, and the Azerbaijani company Iqlim Scientific Production Enterprise.

During the ADEX defence exhibition, Mustafayev presented Aliyev and Defence Minister Zakir Hasanov with the first M4 prototype produced at the facility, explaining the project and its manufacturing process.

Several Israeli defence companies also took part in this year’s ADEX exhibition, including Aeronautics, Plasan, UVision, Bagira and Bird. Ondas, whose Israeli operations have attracted attention, was represented under the leadership of former Mossad chief Dedi Barnea, who serves as the company’s president and chairman.

Elbit Systems, which is Israel's largest private defense corporation, has previously reportedly offered to localize the production of its products in Azerbaijan with local partners.

https://civil.ge/archives/755241.heading: Georgian Foreign Ministry Accuses EU Representatives of Interference After Criticism of Party Ban Proceedings – Civil Georgia
https://civil.ge/archives/755241.body:
Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused EU representatives of interference in internal affairs and an attempt to pressure the court after the European Commission spokesperson criticized the ruling Georgian Dream party’s constitutional lawsuit seeking to ban five major opposition parties.

The ministry said in its October 20 statement that it “expresses concern regarding the latest statements by EU representatives concerning the proceedings before the Constitutional Court of Georgia,” without explicitly mentioning the nature of the proceedings it was referring to.

It “considers that assessments questioning the legitimacy of the proceedings before the Court has examined the case and prejudging the judicial process represent an attempt to exert undue pressure on a constitutional institution and constitute interference in Georgia’s internal affairs, whereas respect for the rule of law requires allowing the Court to examine the case independently, in accordance with the Constitution and applicable legislation,” the ministry added.

The ministry also criticized what it described as “recurring rhetoric and declarations” by EU representatives concerning Georgia’s domestic political and legal developments, arguing that such statements “undermine an objective assessment of ongoing processes and hinder constructive engagement between Georgia and the European Union.”

“The Ministry calls on all relevant representatives to refrain from statements and actions that could prejudge ongoing judicial proceedings or be perceived as interference in the work of independent constitutional institutions, and to uphold the principles of the rule of law, judicial independence and mutual respect,” the statement concluded.

The statement came a day after European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand told Georgian journalist Tamara Nutsubidze during an October 19 midday briefing in Brussels that the EU was “closely following” the constitutional lawsuit.

“These developments, alongside recent legal amendments and earlier statements about banning opposition parties, suggest a troubling instrumentalization of the justice system,” Wigand said. “This risks undermining fundamental freedoms, democratic pluralism and fair political competition.”

Earlier, the European Parliament also criticized the proceedings in an October 8 resolution, where the MEPs called for the immediate withdrawal of Georgian Dream’s lawsuit. The resolution described the proceedings as an attempt to “eliminate legitimate political opposition” and part of a broader strategy aimed at “turning Georgia into a one-party regime by eliminating political pluralism.”

Georgian Dream initially filed the constitutional lawsuit in October 2025, seeking to outlaw the United National Movement (UNM), Lelo/Strong Georgia and Ahali/Coalition for Change. The lawsuit was later expanded in April 2026 to include the Federalists, and again in September to add For Georgia, the only opposition party still represented in Parliament, leading the GD to resubmit the claim each time and thus reset the court’s maximum 9-month deadline to rule on the case.

The latest exchange between Georgian authorities and EU representatives comes ahead of Constitutional Court hearings on the lawsuit, scheduled for October 21-23.

Journalist jailed over Facebook post in Georgia

Popular Georgian TV host Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 30 days’ administrative detention on 19 October over social media posts deemed insulting to government officials.

The lawsuit was filed by the Department for Monitoring Hate Speech and Aggressive Statements, which recently became part of the Interior Ministry. Sanaia was accused of insulting Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and MP Vladimir (Lado) Bozhadze in his Facebook posts and videos.

This is the third sentence handed down to the Formula TV host on similar charges since July this year, and his second term of detention.

Sanaia did not attend the court hearing, saying that prosecuting him for his posts was absurd. Police arrested him at his home.

“They want to force society into silence, but society will never be silent. We will overthrow this regime, however long it takes. This will certainly end in our victory,” Sanaia said as he was being arrested.

The case centres on three social media posts about parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili and ruling-party MP Vladimir Bozhadze.

The posts included censored profanities referring to the two politicians.

In a post on 22 July, shortly before he was detained in an earlier case, Sanaia wrote: “For 14 days, don’t call Shalva [Papuashvili] and Lado [Bozhadze] [censored insult] – when I get out, I’ll deal with that.”

In another post on 5 August, he referred to his earlier remarks, writing: “I wrote that you shouldn’t call Papuashvili and Bozhadze [censored insult], and they arrested me.”

On 24 September, Sanaia published a video address whose title also contained a censored profane reference to Papuashvili. Sanaia has described the proceedings as an attempt to restrict freedom of expression.

The case is being brought under Article 173¹⁶ of Georgia’s Code of Administrative Offences, which penalises insulting a political office-holder. The provision allows for a fine of 2,500 to 6,000 lari ($930–$2,220) or administrative detention for between five and 60 days.

This is the third administrative case against Sanaia. In July, he was fined 6,000 lari and sentenced to 14 days in detention over earlier posts involving the same two politicians.

The Interior Ministry’s Division for Combating Hate Speech began operating on 1 June. It monitors public statements, including social media posts, and refers cases to court. Local media report that the unit often acts without a complaint from the person allegedly insulted. Cases brought by the division have led to dozens of fines and several detentions.

The case comes amid deteriorating relations between Georgia and the West. In November 2024, the government halted EU accession talks until 2028, triggering mass protests. Georgia has also fallen to 135th place out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 Press Freedom Index, down from 77th in 2022.

European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand has commented on the arrest of Vakho Sanaia:

“We have been very vocal in our criticism of Georgian Dream’s actions aimed at suppressing the political opposition, journalists and activists. Unfortunately, they continue to restrict civic space. The Georgian authorities must immediately release all unjustly detained politicians, journalists and activists and repeal repressive legislation.”

The Georgian Charter of Journalistic Ethics described the sentence as unjust, saying the authorities are using legislation and the courts to silence critical voices and restrict independent media.

“Through legislative amendments and, subsequently, the way these amendments are enforced, Georgian Dream has abandoned its obligation to tolerate criticism,” the charter said.

The Media Advocacy Coalition said the third case brought against the same journalist points to a pattern of persecution targeting critical media and dissenting voices. The coalition also expressed solidarity with the Formula TV team.

PEN Georgia called for the detention ruling to be overturned immediately. “In a country where journalists and citizens are jailed for criticising the government, and free speech becomes grounds for punishment, democracy no longer exists,” the organisation said.

Transparency International Georgia said Sanaia was being punished for exposing billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of Georgian Dream and widely seen as Georgia’s shadow ruler, and for supporting the country’s European future.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said obscene language in public was unacceptable and could carry legal consequences.

“Obscenity has nothing to do with expressing an opinion and is not protected by freedom of expression,” he said.

Papuashvili said he did not follow individual cases. According to him, the Interior Ministry’s unit operates automatically, and those targeted often learn about decisions only after they have been made.

He also cited Germany, saying people can face criminal charges for insulting others on social media, including following a personal complaint by the chancellor.

Papuashvili also criticised the EU ambassador, claiming that “he himself promotes hatred” and that “some people may try to win his favour.”

“If he has the audacity to use obscene language in public, he should also have the courage to face the consequences,” Papuashvili said of Sanaia.

The new president of South Ossetia, Marat Kambolov, has ordered an investigation into the legality of the circulation of civilian, service and military firearms, as well as bladed weapons.

The Prosecutor General’s Office is carrying out the president’s order. Kambolov’s fellow villager, Soslanbek Kozhiyev, was recently appointed first deputy prosecutor general.

The authorities will pay particular attention to a practice that took hold under previous presidents: handing out Glock and Beretta pistols left, right and centre under the pretext of awarding them as honours. Smugglers brought the pistols into South Ossetia from Georgia.

Officials often used these supposed “awards” as a cover to sell the weapons to members of the criminal underworld or simply to anyone who wanted one. And plenty of people in South Ossetia want a gun “just in case”. However, Kambolov believes this “tradition”, which dates back to the 1990s, has run its course. He says that civilian gun ownership no longer serves a relevant purpose and that real security risks no longer justify it.

“Today, South Ossetia leads a peaceful life and is building a state governed by the rule of law. In a peaceful state, the law — not tradition, personal merit, official position or private arrangements — must determine the right to own a gun.

The republic has suspended all awards of weapons until the investigation ends. The state must know exactly where each weapon is, to whom and on what grounds it was issued, how it was registered and who is responsible for it,” the president said.

At the same time, he proposes extending permits to possess and carry most types of civilian firearms to ten years, while retaining mandatory checks and periodic permit renewals:

“This approach will allow us to bring order to the firearms register without imposing excessive bureaucracy on law-abiding owners. The republic’s Security Council will make the final decision on this matter, following a proposal from the prosecutor general.”

Gagloev has led South Ossetia for four years, and criticism of his leadership is growing louder.

These measures come amid criminal proceedings against former Interior Minister Erislav Mamiyev and his first deputy, Atsamaz Sagkayev.

Investigators suspect that Sagkayev “gifted” his boss, Mamiyev, a sniper rifle and an assault rifle in 2025 and 2026.

Authorities have opened two criminal cases against Sagkayev on suspicion of “abuse of official powers for personal gain or other personal motives”, an offence under the Criminal Code.

Some Telegram channels claim that over those two years, Sagkayev used the pretext of awarding weapons to sell 400 firearms to unknown buyers.

Both Sagkayev and Mamiyev lost their jobs at the Interior Ministry in August 2026, when Marat Kambolov, then prime minister, launched the first stage of a purge of South Ossetia’s security agencies.

Many consider Erislav Mamiyev a close friend of local crime boss Alexander (Alik) Gagloyev, the brother of former president Alan Gagloyev.

Social media has also circulated claims that Alan Gagloyev and his team planned to use his gangster brother and their friends, armed with weapons presented as “awards”, to hold on to power by force if he lost the 2027 presidential election.

But that scenario never materialised. In mid-2026, the Kremlin itself ousted Gagloyev from the presidency and effectively installed its own envoy, Marat Kambolov, in his place.

friends of Alan Gagloev’s brother, the current president, opened fire on supporters of former president Anatoly Bibilov. The attack took place in broad daylight on a busy street in Tskhinval

The new president is now trying to clean up his predecessor’s “legacy” and deliver on his promise to restore order, a pledge he repeatedly made to the people of South Ossetia over the past several months.

However, Alan Gagloyev was not the only former president involved in illegal arms trafficking. His predecessor, Leonid Tibilov, also had a record of such activity. One case came to light relatively recently, in autumn 2025. The major scandal that erupted at the time also implicated former Interior Minister Akhsar Lavoyev and Russian debt collector Eduard Budantsev, alongside Tibilov.

It emerged that back in December 2015, Budantsev and several former colleagues had exchanged gunfire in central Moscow using award weapons from South Ossetia. He had acquired the weapons through Tibilov and his inner circle.

“The trade in Glocks and Berettas in South Ossetia became a well-oiled operation under Tibilov and his associates. Gagloyev and his people simply continued the lucrative business,” a local expert said on condition of anonymity.

https://www.novinite.com/articles/241143.body:
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán (left), Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova (right)

Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea were creating an unacceptable impression that merchant shipping had become a battlefield, calling for diplomatic action through European and NATO channels to stop military operations.

Petrova made the remarks on BNT where she appeared alongside Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán. Their discussion covered drone attacks in the Black Sea, Russia’s war against Ukraine, diplomacy and prospects for peace, protests across Europe, and relations between Bulgaria and Hungary.

Orbán expressed Hungary’s solidarity with Bulgaria over the attacks in the Black Sea, stressing the importance of protecting shipping routes connecting Europe with other regions, including Central Asia. She warned that disruptions to food supplies could cause serious shortages and insisted that both commercial shipping and the transport of grain through the Black Sea must be secured.

Petrova said the Black Sea was strategically important not only for Bulgaria but also for Europe as a whole. She noted that attacks were taking place beyond Bulgarian waters, creating the impression that commercial vessels had become targets on a battlefield.

“And this is absolutely unacceptable,” Petrova said, adding that Bulgaria was working with its political partners to secure a clear commitment to diplomatic efforts aimed at ending all military operations. She stressed that protection must extend beyond grain shipments to every category of commercial vessel, noting that oil tankers had also been hit near Romania.

Petrova said Bulgaria would pursue the issue through both the EU and NATO, with the aim of reaching an agreement among all Black Sea countries to halt military action in all its forms.

Turning to Ukraine, Orbán said both sides wanted a diplomatic settlement and a swift end to the war, with the goal of achieving a just and lasting peace. She said Hungary’s position largely matched Bulgaria’s, particularly on opposition to sending weapons to Ukraine. Budapest also rejects accelerating Ukraine’s EU accession, favoring a process based on merit.

Petrova agreed that the two countries shared more positions than they differed on the issue. She said diplomacy should play a greater role and Europe should participate actively in efforts to end the war. Ukraine should receive support when it demonstrates progress, she added, noting that both countries had backed opening the next two EU negotiating clusters.

Petrova said a shared emphasis on diplomacy, rather than an exclusive focus on the military dimension of the conflict, was an important point of agreement between Bulgaria and Hungary. She argued that the war’s conclusion must be based on terms negotiated clearly through diplomatic channels by Ukraine and Russia.

“While we can certainly see the roles played by Europe, the United States, and third parties, ultimately, it is the two warring parties themselves that will determine the parameters under which this peace is established,” Petrova said.

She warned that Europe would struggle to secure an outcome favorable to its interests if it were excluded from the negotiations, making its participation essential.

The ministers also discussed unrest in France. Petrova said the situation reflected growing polarization in European societies, which extremist political forces were exploiting.

She distinguished between peaceful demonstrations and the vandalism that followed, describing the latter as unacceptable. Such divisions, she said, were not confined to France and were always destructive. Petrova added that people seeking political change should pursue it through elections rather than vandalism.

Orbán said protesters should be distinguished from those involved in vandalism and looting. She expressed Hungary’s solidarity with France and hope that the authorities would bring the situation under control, while emphasizing that the concerns of demonstrators needed to be heard.

Orbán identified competitiveness as one of Europe’s most pressing challenges, saying people wanted economic growth, security and predictability, along with a strong social welfare system.

She also described relations between Hungary and Bulgaria as stable in political, economic and cultural terms.

The program additionally addressed bilateral ties between Bulgaria and Hungary, EU enlargement, North Macedonia’s path toward the bloc, and shared objectives and priorities.

Bulgaria supports open and constructive dialogue between the European Union (EU) and China, Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said on Monday after meeting with her Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, who is on an official visit to Bulgaria.

The two discussed EU-China relations, among other topics. Bulgaria welcomes the first tangible results of consultations on trade and investment that emerged in October, Petrova added.

Petrova said economic ties were an important part of the partnership between Bulgaria and China and were developing dynamically. She said the two countries sought to ensure that this momentum was sustainable and mutually beneficial. “We discussed speeding up procedures for granting market access to Bulgarian agricultural and food products. Mutual investment is the surest path to closer economic integration, and we see significant untapped potential in this area,” Petrova explained. “We paid particular attention to connectivity between Europe and Asia. In 2027, Bulgaria will host a regional connectivity summit organized jointly with the European Commission. A key focus will be connectivity along the Middle Corridor, as well as between Europe and the countries of the Persian Gulf,” Petrova said.

She also said the positive cooperation in traditional areas such as education, science, culture, sports, youth exchanges and tourism.

Bulgaria’s Foreign Minister said the country valued the visa-free regime for Bulgarian citizens and expressed hope that it would continue. “We support efforts to establish a direct air link between the two countries,” Velislava Petrova added.

Wang said that China is ready to deepen cooperation with Bulgaria in green development and artificial intelligence. He highlighted joint work in energy storage, which, he said, was helping Bulgaria take a leading position in Europe in terms of energy storage capacity.

He added he had held in-depth talks with Petrova and that the two sides had reached a consensus. Wang voiced readiness to develop the strategic partnership, promote connectivity between Europe and Asia, and give fresh impetus to relations between China and the European Union.

The Chinese Foreign Minister highlighted trust, friendship, cooperation and partnership as the main messages of his recent tour of Azerbaijan, Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria. Before visiting Bulgaria, he attended the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia as a special representative of Chinese President Xi Jinping. All four countries participate in and benefit from China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Wang cited the Gobustan photovoltaic power plant in Azerbaijan, the Peljesac Bridge in Croatia, Montenegro’s Bar-Boljare motorway project and energy storage cooperation with Bulgaria as examples of partnerships tailored to national circumstances and citizens’ needs. He voiced China’s readiness to deepen cooperation with all four countries.

Wang also stressed the importance of cultural exchanges between East and West, emphasizing that Bulgaria was home to the Balkans’ first Confucius Institute and first Chinese cultural centre. He said China favoured partnerships over alliances and dialogue over confrontation, adding that the three Balkan countries he visited supported closer China-Europe relations and wanted stronger cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European countries.

China aims to be a reliable, long-term strategic partner for these countries, Wang said, adding that bilateral ties, regional cooperation and China-EU relations could develop in parallel and reinforce one another. He described progress in China-EU trade and investment consultations as evidence that differences could be managed through dialogue. He called for stronger multilateral cooperation, free trade and mutually beneficial economic ties, arguing that openness brings progress while isolation leads to falling behind.

Ahead of the 15th anniversary of the China-Central and Eastern European Countries cooperation mechanism, Wang called for its further development. He also stressed that trust was essential to peace, saying that resolving the war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East required communication, dialogue, consultation and mutual understanding. Following talks with representatives of Israel, Palestine and other Middle Eastern countries at the summit, he said China would continue working to build trust and help resolve international crises and conflicts.

Croatia is strengthen its ties with Southeast Asia, with Foreign Minister Gordan Grlić Radman making the first official visit by a Croatian foreign minister to Cambodia on 19 and 20 October 2026.

The visit coincides with the 30th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries and focused on expanding political and economic cooperation.

During talks with Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn, Grlić Radman discussed opportunities to strengthen cooperation in trade, investment, tourism, connectivity and demining.

He said Croatia was increasingly turning its attention towards Asia following the achievement of key foreign policy objectives, describing the visit as the opening of a new chapter in relations between the two countries.

(Photo:Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs)

The ministers also discussed cooperation between the European Union and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), as well as the importance of defending international law and multilateralism.

Both sides highlighted the potential for closer cooperation between smaller countries based on mutual respect.

A significant part of the visit focused on Croatia’s experience in post-war reconstruction and humanitarian demining.

Grlić Radman met senior Cambodian minister Ly Thuch and took part in a Croatian-Cambodian dialogue on innovation and cooperation in demining.

(Photo:Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs)

Drawing on the experiences of both countries following conflict, the Croatian minister outlined how Croatia had progressed from receiving international assistance to sharing its expertise and technology with other countries, including Ukraine.

Cambodia acknowledged Croatia’s contribution to demining. Croatia announced the completion of its domestic mine-clearance process in March 2026, following decades of work to address the legacy of the 1991–1995 Homeland War.

The discussions highlighted opportunities for the two countries to exchange knowledge and explore further cooperation in this field.

Focus on justice and historical memory

The visit also included stops at Cambodia’s Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum and the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), established with United Nations involvement to prosecute crimes committed by the Khmer Rouge regime.

(Photo:Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs)

At Tuol Sleng, Grlić Radman condemned crimes committed under communist and other totalitarian regimes, stressing the importance of preserving the memory of victims and preventing similar atrocities from recurring.

At the ECCC, he emphasised the importance of prosecuting war crimes, securing justice for victims and combating impunity.

He also referred to Croatia’s experience of the peaceful reintegration of the Danube region under the United Nations Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium (UNTAES).

Meetings with Cambodia’s leadership

During his two-day visit, Grlić Radman was received by Cambodian King Norodom Sihamoni and met Prime Minister Hun Manet, National Assembly President Khuon Sudary and Senate President Hun Sen.

(Photo:Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs)

He also met members of the Croatian community living and working in Cambodia, whose activities contribute to strengthening relations between the two countries.

The visit forms part of Croatia’s wider efforts to develop international partnerships beyond Europe, with economic cooperation, regional connectivity and the exchange of expertise among the areas offering potential for closer Croatian-Cambodian relations.

Negotiations are at an advanced stage on a deal worth around €150 million between Israeli defence companies Israel Shipyards and Rafael and the Republic of Cyprus, for the supply of naval vessels equipped with advanced weapons systems, according to a report in the Israeli financial newspaper Calcalist.

The agreement is expected to be signed in the coming weeks, once the terms have been finalised between the defence ministries of Israel and Cyprus.

The agreement currently taking shape is expected to give a substantial boost to defence cooperation between Israel and Cyprus, while at the same time expanding the capabilities of the Cypriot National Guard at sea.

It also highlights the two countries' determination to deepen their strategic relationship at a time when security and stability in the Eastern Mediterranean are gaining increased importance.

Under the planned programme, Israel Shipyards will be responsible for supplying the naval vessels, which will be fitted with weapons systems made by Rafael.

The agreement is being promoted through a Government-to-Government (G2G) cooperation framework, giving the initiative a broader institutional and strategic dimension.

Cooperation between the two Israeli companies and Cyprus does not start from scratch. Less than a decade ago, Israel Shipyards supplied the Republic of Cyprus with a patrol vessel to protect its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).

The vessel is equipped with radar, command-and-control systems and two Typhoon naval weapon stations.

At the same time, Israel Shipyards and Rafael have worked together on other defence programmes, including agreements involving Azerbaijan and the Philippines. The possible new deal with Cyprus would therefore build on the existing know-how and cooperation within Israel's defence industry.

The naval agreement under negotiation is part of a broader framework for strengthening defence and diplomatic ties between Israel and Cyprus. The presence of Israeli systems within Cyprus's defence architecture is also indicative of this trend.

According to the report, Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) has supplied Cyprus with the Barak MX air and missile defence system. The system was shown publicly at a military parade in Nicosia in early October, during events marking the 66th anniversary of the independence of the Republic of Cyprus.

Although Israel has not officially confirmed the agreement, the public display of the system highlighted the breadth of the technological and defence links between the two countries.

Strengthening these ties takes on particular significance against the backdrop of regional rivalries and tensions with Turkey, as well as the wider repercussions of the protracted conflict in the Middle East.

The defence rapprochement between Israel and Cyprus is linked to Israel's wider strategic cooperation with Greece, creating a network of relations that carries particular weight for security in the Eastern Mediterranean.

In August, Israel and Greece signed a 3 billion euro agreement for the "Achilles Shield" programme, aimed at creating a multi-layered Greek air defence network using systems from Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries.

These parallel initiatives reflect the growing importance of defence cooperation between the three countries, both in terms of armaments programmes and in terms of strategic coordination.

For Cyprus in particular, the deepening of relations with Israel opens up prospects for upgrading its operational capabilities and strengthening cooperation in areas of advanced defence technology.

Beyond the supply of naval vessels and weapons systems, Israeli defence sources quoted by Calcalist believe the agreement could open the way to further commercial partnerships, including in the field of defence industrial production.

Such a development could give the Israel-Cyprus partnership a long-term character, going beyond a one-off arms procurement and creating additional opportunities for the transfer of know-how and the development of joint activities.

Rafael and Israel Shipyards have not commented on the report or on the agreement that is currently being drawn up.

According to Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov, Europe must take a decisive role in supporting Ukraine in light of criticism coming from the United States.

According to Vseviov, the situation in Ukraine is difficult because people's hope that the war will one day end is under constant attack.

"The longer the war has gone on, the harder it has become for both sides fighting it. The same applies to those supporting the warring parties and we feel all of this here in Europe as well. The burden keeps growing. Fortunately, the same is true in Russia because the frantic activity we are seeing there is nothing more than a sign of desperation. But things are also difficult for Ukrainians, not only because Russia is deliberately destroying civilian infrastructure, as it has been doing for years, but because their hope that the light at the end of the tunnel will one day become a reality and that they will be able to live normal European lives is under constant attack," Vseviov said.

According to the secretary general, however, the news coming out of the United States offers little additional hope. For Europeans, this means they must take matters into their own hands and support Ukraine, because ultimately it is not just Ukraine's fate that is being decided there, but Europe's as well.

Conflicting information has emerged from the U.S. and no one knows for certain or is willing to say who restricted Starlink connectivity. There are also conflicting reports about whether intelligence sharing has been suspended.

"What I can say about technology is that if we cannot be certain we will be able to use it with 100 percent reliability at the most critical moment, then we clearly cannot trust it. That does not mean we should not use the technology — we certainly can, but we cannot rely on it. Now, are these various reports true or is there genuinely conflicting information? I trust what the Ukrainians say most because they are the ones using the technology directly. When I last checked, just before coming into the studio, it appeared there were indeed some disruptions, but there did not seem to have been a complete shutdown. The truth is probably somewhere in between," Vseviov said.

According to Vseviov, the more important question is whether the United States can be counted on to use its power to support the victim against the aggressor.

"It seems the answer is unequivocal — no, it cannot. Hopefully, the U.S. will not side with the aggressor against the victim, but clearly, at present, it is not supporting the victim. We in Europe must therefore fill the gaps," the secretary general said.

"I would point out that when legislation concerning Russian aggression has been discussed in the U.S. Congress, support for Ukraine has been overwhelming and bipartisan. The butcher Putin is not popular among the American people. Of course, elections are approaching in America and all politicians must take public opinion into account. There are few situations in international affairs and politics today that are as black and white as Russia's aggression against Ukraine. There is a clear aggressor and a clear victim, a clear tyrant and a clear free society. Such things matter in the United States and they matter to ordinary people on the street who may not follow foreign policy on a daily basis. Of course, domestic issues ultimately determine election outcomes, but people's desire to be on the right side of history is also a decisive factor," Vseviov explained.

"Throughout its history, America has contributed to addressing various problems around the world partly because it wants to be on the right side of history. I think that ultimately, as Winston Churchill famously said, the United States will make all the right choices," Vseviov added.

The question, however, is when those right choices will be made because this is a matter of practical policy with real stakes and its success is measured not only in abstract or intangible terms but also in human lives every single day, the secretary general said.

Vseviov believes that the money Ukraine needs to defend itself and keep the country running ahead of a difficult winter will probably be found.

"But money is not the main issue. If I were to single out two of the most important things to add, the first would naturally be to prevent the situation from being made worse. By this, we mean above all the need to support Ukraine if it rejects any 21st-century deals resembling Munich or Yalta. Just recently, Putin proposed that three presidents — Putin himself, Trump and Xi Jinping — could meet to discuss the Ukraine question. We know that when Putin puts the Ukraine question on the table, he is putting not only Ukraine but all of Europe on the table as well. So, first, we must prevent things from getting worse and, second, we must ensure that Ukrainians have hope and a future. One thing that is clearly in Europe's hands is the European Union's enlargement process. This must be based entirely on facts and Ukraine's progress and we must maintain high standards for Ukraine," the secretary general said.

"However, while maintaining those high standards, we must also ensure that the process moves forward. I would say these two things are at least as important as money. And, of course, we must continue putting pressure on Russia," Vseviov added.
