PARIS (AP) — Paris police issued an overnight curfew on Monday in two areas of the French capital, after a weekend marred by France’s worst rioting in years that targeted city halls, other public buildings and thousands of businesses across the country.

The order aims to protect “people and property from the violence and looting,” the Paris police statement said.

The curfew prohibits anyone from entering or remaining on the Place de la République, where rioting took place Saturday, and the shopping neighborhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.

The curfew will be in effect from 11 p.m. Monday until 6 a.m. Tuesday. In addition, gatherings and demonstrations are banned from 8 p.m., the Paris police said.

AP correspondent Charles de Ledesma reports that French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is calling for curfews following violent protests over the weekend.

Earlier Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had called for “very limited” and “localized” curfews.

In northern France, local authorities imposed a curfew for children and teenagers under age 18 in several cities, including Lille, starting from Monday and for the next two days from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. Nice, on the French Riviera, also imposed an overnight curfew for minors from 9 p.m.

Lecornu defended police handling of the unrest, saying that “despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle.”

He said that details of the curfews would be announced later Monday after consultations with mayors.

Mass protests in France are often tainted by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. Saturday’s unrest recalled the riots that followed the fatal police shooting of a teenager in 2023, when authorities imposed local curfews, and violence during the yellow vest movement that began in 2018 over fuel prices and broader economic grievances.

The prime minister’s instructions come after Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation Sunday. But President Emmanuel Macron refused it “given the need for continued command of law enforcement in the current context,” Macron’s office said in a statement Monday.

He instructed Nuñez “to take all necessary steps to ensure full transparency about the failures in planning and intelligence-gathering that led to the violence,” the statement said.

Macron also asked for the introduction of “new policing tactics on the ground as quickly as possible” to put an end to the violence.

On Sunday evening, groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities. That followed the violence during nationwide protests Saturday against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 2,400 people were arrested across the country.

Authorities estimated Monday that at least 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted in several cities.

In Marseille, the prefect banned any protest or other gatherings from noon to 8 p.m. Monday.

“I submitted my resignation because I am responsible for everything that is happening,” Nuñez said on France Inter radio. “Now the real issue is ensuring that this doesn’t happen again. … We obviously need to be better at anticipating the kind of mobilization that is unfolding.”

Nuñez blamed the violence on “hordes of troublemakers and looters” and “far-left activists,” and said that police strategy needs to be adapted “in the face of extremely mobile groups.”

Authorities said that groups of hundreds of people sought confrontations with police and targeted public buildings, including city halls and other public offices.

Nuñez acknowledged that authorities had “lost control” in some major cities on Saturday.

“You can’t look shopkeepers in the eye when hundreds of businesses have been looted and say we haven’t lost control in some of these major cities,” Nuñez said.

Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.

On Monday, cleanup crews and firefighters cleared shattered glass and other debris from the streets of Paris.

Ouri Zagoury, owner of a video game shop near Paris’ Place de la République, said that he closed the store Saturday afternoon, but then saw looters forcing their way in on surveillance cameras.

“There were so many people coming in and out. And even though I called the police, they said not to intervene, that they would come, but they never did, which is another problem,” Zagoury said.

Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally party, pointed to the government’s failure to prevent violence.

“The government has failed, the head of state has failed in his essential duty of protecting the French people,” he told reporters at the party’s headquarters.

“I call on the people of France now, beyond their right to protest, to use their voting power,” Bardella said. He is campaigning alongside far-right leader Marine Le Pen, whose polling numbers have suggested for months that she’s the front-runner in next spring’s presidential election.

Tom Nouvian, Oleg Cetinic and Nicolas Garriga in Paris, and Lorne Cook in Brussels, contributed to this report.

PARIS, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Overnight curfews ​in violence-hit zones of France's biggest cities helped bring respite from the nation's worst unrest in years, the government said, ahead of more protests planned for ‌the weekend.

Buoyed by protests in France, crowds have also taken to the streets in other countries, including Italy and Albania, where similar anger over living conditions has led to clashes.

Reeling from a weekend of violence, the French government tried to reassure the public it had learned from security shortcomings that left the centres of cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon largely unprotected from rioters and looters moving in after demonstrations.

"The targeted curfews have contributed to ​the calm of last night," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said in a post on X, adding they may be extended further into the week where needed.

In central Paris, police ​emptied and guarded the Place de la Republique overnight, with a helicopter overhead. In Lille, in the north, where the curfew only applied to ⁠minors, officers patrolled the city centre, checking bypassers' identities.

Marseille mayor Benoit Payan said there would be curfews for minors around the commercial areas hardest hit by the weekend's riots, starting Tuesday ​night.

High-school pupil strikes and demonstrations against falling standards and growing dilapidation have converged with a broader outpouring of anger at rising prices and the sense that health, housing and welfare needs are also ​no longer being met.

Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin told BFM television that 149 people held at the weekend were in detention awaiting trial. In a separate TV appearance on Monday evening, he said around 2,500 remained in custody for questioning.

The unrest has stoked a febrile political atmosphere six months from a presidential election, with candidates from the far-right and hard-left leading the pack, according to opinion polls.

French government bond yields – the ​premium investors demand for holding the country's debt – climbed further on Tuesday over fears of more protests, with ten-year debt reaching its highest yield level in 24 years.

Scrambling to find a way ​out of the crisis and re-centre attention on passing a budget bill, Lecornu has invited political parties from both his government and the opposition to meet for consultations on Thursday.

Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally ‌said it ⁠would send a representative. It remained unclear if the hard-left France Unbowed party led by Jean-Luc Melenchon would also join.

Separately, groups identifying themselves as "Gilets Jaunes" (Yellow Vests) called for scattered protest ​actions against spiralling fuel costs.

The yellow vest ​movement, largely inactive in recent years, sprung ⁠up in 2018 during Macron's first term over plans to raise petrol taxes. Weekly traffic blockades and waves of street violence continued for months until the government got its cheque book out.

Lecornu vowed on Monday that the government would learn lessons from last weekend's protests and ensuing ​chaos.

"There were things that went well, and things that were screwed up," he said. "My determination to restore order is absolute."

France's main labour unions, ​including the CGT – often the ⁠driving force behind large organised demonstrations – have not joined the calls for protests on Saturday.

In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet was due to discuss a response to two days of unrest in the heart of Milan at the weekend and clashes in other northern cities including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin.

That response would include the dispatch of 500 soldiers to help "defend Milan", Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini ⁠said.

Hungary and Slovakia are calling for greater flexibility and more EU funding as the bloc prepares to end Russian energy imports in 2027, warning that replacing existing supplies could prove costly for Central Europe.

Hungary and Slovakia are urging Brussels to ease the rules surrounding the phase-out of Russian gas and provide more funding to expand regional energy infrastructure, Euronews reports. They argue that their geographical position and dependence on existing supply routes make it harder and more expensive to diversify their energy sources.

Under the European Union’s plans, Russian energy imports to Central Europe are due to end in 2027, raising concerns in both countries about energy security, industrial competitiveness and the cost of replacing existing supplies.

Slovakia has historically served as an entry point for Russian oil and gas, but it now risks becoming a destination at the end of alternative supply routes, alongside Hungary, as the EU moves away from Russian energy.

Speaking at a press conference in Bratislava attended by European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen, Slovak Deputy Prime Minister Denisa Saková called for discussions with the European Commission on how the next EU funding period could address the region’s needs.

“We would like to discuss with the European Commission how the next EU funding period and the availability of EU funds can meet our needs, particularly regarding the expansion of oil and gas infrastructure in the Visegrád Four region,” Saková said.

Saková also stressed the importance of preparing new supply agreements ahead of the 2027 deadline, arguing that energy security requires clear rules for delivering oil and gas throughout the region.

The latest appeal follows pressure from all four Visegrád countries at the European Council summit on 15–16 October. They called on EU leaders to reconsider measures intended to ease electricity costs across Central Europe. Their demands included greater flexibility in the ongoing review of the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS), the bloc’s carbon market, and postponing the introduction of its second phase, ETS2, until 2030.

The countries argue that high energy prices are making it harder for their industries to invest in electrification, the transition from fossil fuels to electricity-powered processes and technologies. The US-Israeli war against Iran has contributed to rising energy prices, adding to the pressure on households and businesses across Europe.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.body:
Italy’s government will dispatch 500 army troops to “defend Milan” after two days ⁠of unrest that saw demonstrators ⁠clash with police, ​loot shops and vandalise property, deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday.

The deployment is expected to be included in a package of security measures to be approved at ⁠a cabinet meeting expected on Tuesday, and comes as shops in central Milan closed early and boarded up their windows, fearing a fresh outbreak of violence in Italy’s financial capital.

“From words to action: 500 more ⁠troops to defend Milan,” Salvini, head of the co-ruling right-wing League party, wrote on social media.

Most stores in Milan’s Via ​Montenapoleone luxury shopping district, home to brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior, had removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution, while police patrolled the street and a handful of tourists looked on.

Several hundred hooded ‌protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze and looted shops in the city centre over the weekend after an initially peaceful demonstration on Saturday over poor public services and rising costs.

Among the stores ransacked were sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed. Clothing brands Levi’s and Under Armour, as well as Decathlon, covered their shop windows with cardboard and wooden panels.

Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who ‌faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs on Monday to discuss the situation.

“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X.

As part of the planned crackdown, the Corriere della Sera newspaper said Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, while bringing forward some provisions contained in an existing security bill currently being examined by parliament.

Italian ⁠police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of ​those taken to police stations, 32 were ​arrested, including 23 minors and 13 ​foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.

The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday.

The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.

https://nltimes.nl/2026/10/20/ing-allowe.body:
The court in Amsterdam has banned ING from terminating its banking relationship with Gazprom in a summary proceeding filed by the Russian energy conglomerate. The Dutch bank must continue offering banking services to Gazprom until the Russian company can open a European bank account elsewhere, the court ruled.

ING notified Gazprom in August 2025 that the bank intended to close its accounts. The bank agreed to give the Russian company time to open another European bank account. On October 1 of this year, its patience ran out, and it sought to terminate the contract. Gazprom could not find another European bank willing to do business with it, so it filed summary proceedings against ING’s intentions.

The Dutch bank gave various reasons for why it wanted to cut ties with Gazprom in the court case. ING argued that it has sought to avoid having clients with ties to Russia since the country invaded Ukraine. The European Union has sanctioned numerous Russian companies, and while Gazprom is not on that list yet, the bank still considers the company a risk.

ING pointed out that Gazprom is part of the Gazprom Group, which is controlled by the Russian state, and operates within the energy sector. The bank therefore considers it likely that Gazprom could end up on the sanctions list. The bank argued that a sanctions risk can also give rise to a money laundering risk.

ING also fears reputational damage from continuing to do business with an energy company with ties to the Russian government. The bank pointed out that Dutch media has repeatedly reported on ING’s former and current business relationships with Russian entities, and that these reports result in parliamentary questions and public indignation.

Gazprom argued that it was unable to find another European bank account, and without the ING account, it would not be able to fulfill its obligations to the British and Dutch tax authorities, among others.

The court ruled in Gazprom’s favor, pointing out that the company is not subject to sanctions and ING did not sufficiently prove that it poses a money laundering risk. “Furthermore, the preliminary relief judge is of the provisional opinion that Gazprom has made sufficient efforts to open a bank account elsewhere. While it is true that Gazprom could potentially have made further attempts—as ING has argued—it is highly unlikely that such efforts would be successful, given that Gazprom is part of the Russian Gazprom Group and that the current geopolitical climate works to its disadvantage,” the court said in its ruling.

The court forbade ING from terminating its banking relationship with Gazprom until the Russian company has opened another European bank account. Because ING lost, it is also responsible for the legal costs amounting to €2,324.57.

President Nicușor Dan reaffirmed Romania’s commitment to institutional balance, transparency, and European democratic standards during talks with a Venice Commission delegation. The meeting addressed the rule of law, the role of democratic institutions, and respect for constitutional principles, he announced.

The delegation from the European Commission for Democracy through Law, better known as the Venice Commission, was led by its president, Marta Cartabia. Its visit coincided with the second edition of a rule-of-law forum held in Romania.

Cartabia and the delegation also met interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan at Victoria Palace in Bucharest. Their talks focused on the justice system and the need to rebuild public confidence in state institutions, the government announced.

“The quality of justice is closely linked to the quality of legislation, but also to its interpretation,” Bolojan said. “If there is no consistency, balance, and predictability in decisions, citizens’ trust in state institutions declines.”

The prime minister thanked the Venice Commission for its expertise and continuing support, adding that Romania still needs the partnership.

During the meeting, Marta Cartabia presented Ilie Bolojan with a copy of the commission’s updated Rule of Law Checklist. The document provides criteria intended to support objective, transparent, and comparable assessments of countries’ adherence to rule-of-law principles.

The Venice Commission is an advisory body of the Council of Europe that provides constitutional and legal expertise to member states.

Prime minister-designate Luca Niculescu will present his proposed government and governing program to Romania’s Parliament on Tuesday, October 20. The joint session of the Chamber of Deputies and Senate is scheduled to begin at 2 p.m.

Niculescu’s proposed 18-member cabinet includes 11 ministers from the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and seven independents.

PSD, the National Liberal Party (PNL), the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR), the national minorities group, and the United for Romania parliamentary group have announced their support for the cabinet. Together, they could deliver 279 votes, comfortably above the 233 required for confirmation, Hotnews.ro noted.

On the other hand, the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) and the reformist Save Romania Union (USR) have said they will vote against the proposed government. PNL and UDMR have signed agreements with Luca Niculescu, although they will not hold ministerial positions in the proposed cabinet and intend to move into opposition.

Under parliamentary procedure, Luca Niculescu will present his ministers and governing program before lawmakers debate the proposal. Deputies and senators will then vote by secret ballot, with an absolute majority of all lawmakers required for the government to take office.

President Nicușor Dan nominated Niculescu for prime minister on October 5. He is the fourth nominee since Liberal leader Ilie Bolojan’s government was removed by a no-confidence motion on May 5.

The first nominee, Eugen Tomac, withdrew before seeking Parliament’s approval. The following two nominees, Adrian Veștea and Siegfried Mureșan, failed to secure sufficient support in confidence votes.

If confirmed, the Luca Niculescu cabinet would end more than five months in which Romania has been governed without a fully empowered executive.

Downing Street has hit back at US defence secretary Pete Hegseth after he belittled the efforts of America’s coalition allies during the Afghanistan war.

Number 10 said Hegseth was “wrong” to diminish the role played by international forces in a conflict which cost the lives of 457 UK personnel.

It is the latest sign of strained transatlantic relations after a split between Donald Trump’s administration and Western allies over the Ukraine war.

Responding to Hegseth’s comments, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's official spokesman said: “Frankly, the facts speak for themselves when it comes to the UK’s and Nato’s contribution to Afghanistan, thousands of British and allied families made huge sacrifices to play their significant parts in that war and uphold our values.

“And more than 450 British personnel never returned.

“Their sacrifice and that of other Nato forces was made in the service of collective security and in response to an attack on our ally.

“We are incredibly proud of our armed forces and their service and sacrifice will never be forgotten, and it is wrong to diminish their role.”

In a speech on Saturday Hegseth said: “I was a captain in Afghanistan and we would go to the headquarters in Kabul and there would be 50 flags at the headquarters.

“It was a beautiful thing to see, 50 different countries contributing to the Nato alliance and the ISAF (International Security Assistance Force) mission there.

“Except there were maybe five that contributed, it was actually closer to one or two that by the end were actually involved in kinetic operations.

“In fact the patch ‘ISAF’, we joked it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting’. Which is sort of a joke but it’s demoralising when you feel like it’s not burden sharing, it’s actually a burden.”

It is not the first time the UK has clashed with the Trump administration over the Afghan conflict, which came after Nato’s Article 5 mutual defence provision was triggered for the first time in the wake of the September 11 attacks on the US.

US president Trump’s suggestion Nato allied troops “stayed a little off the front lines” in Afghanistan resulted in a furious backlash across the alliance, with then prime minister Sir Keir Starmer describing the comments as “insulting and frankly appalling”.

Meanwhile Trump’s decision to import diesel from Russia and his suggestion Volodymyr Zelenskyy should be replaced as Ukraine’s leader have contributed to another low point in relations between Washington and European capitals.

The prime minister's spokesman said: “Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies.

“And we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine in its fight against Russian aggression and to defend itself against Russian attacks.”

In the Commons, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Ukraine needed to be involved in any discussions about its future.

Streeting was responding to a question by Liberal Democrats MP Edward Morello (West Dorset) about a proposed meeting between China, Russia and the US to decide Kyiv’s future.

Streeting said: “We support the diplomatic track that is being promoted by the Americans with a view to bring together the Ukrainians and negotiators from Russia to bring an end to this war.

“Our position is clear and was relayed directly by me in Washington last week. There can be no decision about the Ukrainians without the Ukrainians, that peace has to be acceptable to them, and that we will back Ukraine to the hilt.”

https://www.reuters.com/world/us/iran-pr.body:
DUBAI, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end ​the war.

Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to ‌break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.

"Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," one of the officials said. "The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory."

Tehran analyst Saeed Leylaz said that, by prolonging the talks, "Iran is influencing the US election without taking any unlawful action".

The war, which began in February when the US and its ally Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive ​Trump’s approval rating to a record low as polls suggest that Americans worried about high gasoline prices will punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections.

Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil ​prices to drop after the elections, but has not offered a detailed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global ⁠energy shipping route effectively closed by Iran since the war began.

Iranian attacks both threatened and real have kept ship traffic through the strait to a trickle, while a US maritime blockade and trade sanctions have cut ​off Iran's oil export revenues and exacerbated growing domestic economic woes.

With Tehran refusing to make concessions it believes could benefit Trump politically, there is little chance of a breakthrough before the elections, the officials said.

Under pressure from ​Israel, Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme - which Iran says is purely peaceful and Western powers allege has military dimensions - on the table from the outset.

For its part, Tehran insists that its conditions under a "seven-day plan" must be met before nuclear negotiations begin. And it offers no prospect of giving up the leverage over the Strait of Hormuz that the conflict prompted it to seize.

Iran's Foreign Ministry and the US White House did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.

Iran’s proposal, conveyed through Qatari mediators, offered to reopen the strait within seven days, albeit under Iranian control, provided that Washington lifted its maritime blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets and ended ​hostilities on all fronts.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the offer remained on the table, with messages being exchanged through mediators.

Tehran's view that Washington cannot be trusted to commit to diplomacy stems from the attacks on ‌Iran that ⁠have derailed previous negotiations, one Iranian official said.

In June 2025, an Israeli attack wrecked plans for a sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks in Oman. And last February, the US and Israel launched their war just after another round of talks ended, with further technical discussions scheduled.

Maintaining a state somewhere between war and peace through the US midterms allows Iran to sustain pressure on Washington while reiterating its commitment to diplomacy.

Trump has said the US will not bomb Iran again before November 3. However, the officials said Tehran continues to expect that bombing will resume, sooner or later.

Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute ​in Washington, said the clerical establishment clearly wanted to ​hurt Trump politically.

"But the fundamental issue is ⁠that Tehran believes that Trump is interested in regime change ... and following Israeli Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu’s policy of seeking to bring down Iran’s ruling establishment," he said.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Monday, three Israeli officials said, in an unannounced visit to Israel a week before a parliamentary election in ​which Netanyahu's position is at risk.

Iran’s strategy of keeping negotiations alive without rushing towards agreement comes at ​a cost.

Prolonged uncertainty is weighing ⁠on Iran’s already crippled economy and wearing down public patience. Thousands were killed at the turn of the year when the security forces crushed spiralling anti-government protests.

Annual inflation hit 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran, and the rial currency has fallen nearly 35% against the dollar since Washington reapplied its naval blockade in July.

Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 ⁠barrels per day ​at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5, according to energy intelligence platform Vortexa.

But the leadership's ​distrust of Washington extends beyond the current conflict to existential concerns. Iran believes the US has repeatedly broken agreements even when Tehran honoured its commitments, Leylaz said, leaving little confidence that any comprehensive deal would endure.

“Reaching a sustainable deal with the US, even after ​the Trump administration, is no longer possible because of the deepened distrust,” Leylaz said. "Nothing will go back to the pre-war status quo."

https://www.iranintl.com/en/202610205886.heading: Iran Air chief says 30 to 40 operational aircraft destroyed in war | Iran International
https://www.iranintl.com/en/202610205886.body:
Between 30 and 40 of Iran’s operational aircraft were destroyed during the war, while another 70 to 80 were hit, Iran Air chief executive Taher Abdolhai said on Monday.

Abdolhai said Iran had a little over 300 aircraft in total, but only around 130 to 140 were operational before the latest losses, according to Nournews, a media outlet close to Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.

He said the scale of damage varied. Some aircraft were hit by missiles and suffered holes in their fuselages, while one Iran Air aircraft was “completely pulverized.”

Wartime losses cut into an already limited fleet

The figures suggest the war significantly reduced an aviation fleet that was already constrained by sanctions, aging aircraft and difficulties obtaining spare parts.

Abdolhai’s estimate is higher than some earlier figures given by Iranian officials. The secretary of Iran’s Association of Airlines had previously estimated that about 20 aircraft suffered serious damage.

Mohammadreza Rezaei Kouchi, head of parliament’s Civil Commission, had separately said around 50 aircraft were damaged and 10 destroyed.

It remains unclear how many of the damaged aircraft can be repaired and returned to service.

Sanctions have long constrained Iran’s aviation sector

Iran’s commercial aviation industry has for years faced restrictions on buying aircraft, sourcing parts, carrying out maintenance and receiving services at some foreign airports.

Abdolhai said those restrictions had made it harder for Iran Air to maintain its fleet and had also cut the airline off from some profitable markets.

The wartime losses have added another layer of pressure by shrinking the pool of aircraft available for commercial flights and reducing the industry’s ability to preserve routes and revenue.

Final scale of damage remains unclear

Abdolhai did not give a final estimate for the financial cost of the losses or say how many damaged aircraft were beyond repair.

The differing figures offered by Iranian officials also make the full scale of the damage difficult to establish independently.

https://www.dailysabah.com/world/mid-eas.body:
Iran warned Tuesday it will retaliate against any U.S. military strike, dismissing claims that Washington messaged Tehran expecting it to refrain from responding.

Speaking at his weekly press conference, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei described suggestions that the U.S. could attack Iran without retaliation as an "illusion."

He rejected claims Washington had sent a message urging Iran to refrain from responding to a potential U.S. attack.

Baghaei said Tehran had demonstrated it would answer any military strike, adding that "If our response is not stronger, it will certainly be equal."

The spokesperson stressed that the era of the U.S. attacking and withdrawing without consequences was over.

His remarks came in response to claims of a possible U.S. attack on Pickaxe Mountain (Kuh-e Kolang) in Iran.

Baghaei also warned that Iran remained prepared for another Israeli attack, saying the country was not experiencing peace.

Responding to media reports that Israeli officials had discussed another war against Iran with regional parties, he said Tehran was constantly assessing potential threats.

"We live with this possibility and face it day and night," he said, citing the continuing U.S. naval blockade and threats against Iran as reasons for military readiness.

He said Iranian forces had learned from the past two years and were prepared to repel any assault.

Baghaei said Tehran had not entered nuclear negotiations with Washington and thus had no details of such talks to discuss with Russia or other countries.

"We have not entered nuclear negotiations with Washington to discuss their details with other parties," he said.

He rejected speculation that Iran had softened its positions on the nuclear issue, stressing Tehran remained committed to its principles and national interests.

The spokesperson said Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s visit to Tehran was part of regular consultations between the two countries.

He noted the visit had been planned for months and aimed to discuss bilateral relations and regional and international developments.

Baghaei said discussions covered the Caucasus, Europe, the Ukraine conflict, the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program.

He said Russia had played an important role in previous negotiations that led to the 2015 nuclear agreement and continued to offer to help reduce tensions.

Baghaei also dismissed remarks by U.S. officials regarding Iran’s relations with Russia and China, saying Tehran would continue developing ties with both countries regardless of Washington's rhetoric.

He said Iran's cooperation with Moscow and Beijing was based on mutual interests, stressing Tehran understood both countries pursued their own national priorities.

Referring to U.S. President Donald Trump’s remarks, Baghaei said Iranian officials would not engage with such rhetoric, adding sometimes it was better to let others remain in their "illusions."

Baghaei said Tehran would continue pursuing diplomatic opportunities despite its longstanding distrust of Washington.

He accused the U.S. of repeatedly violating its commitments, including since its withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018.

However, he stressed Iran's diplomatic institutions could not abandon negotiations solely because of previous experiences.

"If there is even the slightest possibility diplomacy can prevent an escalation of tensions, we must pursue that path," he said.

Baghaei added Iran's priority remained protecting its national interests and security, whether through diplomacy or military defense.

The spokesperson said a recent message received from the U.S. was "insufficient and incomplete," adding Tehran had already communicated its position to Washington.

He said Iran's seven demands were neither new nor unreasonable, arguing they had already been included in the June understanding between the two countries.

Baghaei cited lifting the U.S. naval blockade and ending hostilities on all fronts among Tehran’s demands, describing them as legitimate and reasonable.

He said Washington needed to make a decision on these issues before diplomatic efforts could move forward.

Baghaei blamed continued U.S. military actions for insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz, calling on the United Nations to help address the situation.

Responding to a question regarding humanitarian shipments, including agricultural supplies and food production materials, he said Tehran had consistently supported efforts to facilitate humanitarian deliveries.

However, he argued the underlying causes of insecurity in the strategic waterway required addressing.

"The cause of insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is clear: the continuation of U.S. interventionist and aggressive actions," he said.

Baghaei urged the U.N. to take steps to prevent Washington from continuing what Tehran considers destabilizing actions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf.

The spokesperson also rejected a resolution adopted at an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) foreign ministers' meeting in Baghdad expressing solidarity with Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

He said Iran had formally opposed the resolution and did not consider it a valid OIC decision, citing what he called failure to follow the organization's procedural rules.

Baghaei said Tehran also prevented the inclusion of two paragraphs regarding Yemen in the meeting's final declaration, arguing their wording would deepen divisions among Muslim countries.

He said the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen should be resolved through dialogue and reconciliation rather than military force.

"The issue of Yemen cannot be resolved through force," he said.

Baghaei called on neighboring countries to prevent foreign powers from using their territory and military facilities to threaten or attack other states.

He said preventing such activities was essential to establishing lasting regional security and maintaining good-neighborly relations.

The spokesperson also accused Israel’s policies and territorial expansion of fueling regional instability.

He said the war in Gaza had not ended the suffering of Palestinians and reiterated Tehran’s criticism of U.S. and European support for Israel.

استمرار أنشطته وتعاظم قوته العسكرية. 🔸 في كانون الأول (ديسمبر) 2025، طُلب من الجيش اللبناني، عبر الآلية الأمريكية، التعامل مع منشأة عسكرية في منطقة كفرا بجنوب لبنان، كان تنظيم حزب الله الإرهابي يستخدمها لتخزين وسائل قتالية. وفي وقت لاحق، أعلن الجيش اللبناني أنه اتخذ الإجراءات اللازمة بشأن هذه المنشأة. 🔸 إلا أنه بعد مرور عدة أشهر على هذا الإعلان، تبيّن أن حزب الله واصل نشاطه داخل المنشأة، وأن عناصره عمدوا إلى نقل وسائل قتالية ومعدات عسكرية منها بهدف الاحتفاظ بها والحفاظ على قدرات التنظيم العسكرية. وبذلك، ظلّت المنشأة متاحة لاستخدام حزب الله لأغراضه العسكرية، رغم مرور عدة أشهر على إعلان الجيش اللبناني اتخاذ الإجراءات اللازمة بشأنها. 🔸 وتكشف المشاهد المرفقة عناصر من حزب الله وهم يحمّلون وسائل قتالية كانت مخزّنة داخل المنشأة على متن شاحنة، في محاولة لنقلها من الموقع والاحتفاظ بها ضمن ترسانة التنظيم العسكرية. 🔸 وعقب رصد هذا النشاط، أغارت قوات جيش الدفاع الإسرائيلي على الشاحنة ودمّرتها، بما في ذلك الوسائل القتالية التي أُخرجت من المنشأة وحُمّلت على متنها. 🔸 ويُظهر المشهد أنه رغم إعلان الجيش اللبناني معالجة المنشأة، استمرّ نشاط عناصر حزب الله فيها، حيث حاولوا نقل وسائل قتالية ومعدات عسكرية منها للاحتفاظ بها. 🔸 وترصد شعبة الاستخبارات العسكرية في جيش الدفاع الإسرائيلي حالات قامت فيها جهات من داخل الجيش اللبناني بالتنسيق مع حزب الله بشأن أنشطة إنفاذ الترتيبات الأمنية، على نحو ساهم في محاولات منع هذه الأنشطة أو تأخيرها أو إحباطها، وأتاح لحزب الله الاستعداد مسبقًا لإخلاء الوسائل القتالية ونقلها من المنطقة. 🔸 يتحمّل الجيش اللبناني مسؤولية ضمان التنفيذ الكامل والدقيق لجميع المهام الموكلة إليه. 🔸 ويؤكد جيش الدفاع الإسرائيلي أنه يتوقع من الجيش اللبناني اتخاذ إجراءات أكثر حزمًا وفعالية للوفاء بمسؤولياته، ومنع وجود الوسائل القتالية والبنى التحتية العسكرية التابعة لتنظيم حزب الله الإرهابي في جنوب لبنان. 🔸 ويواصل جيش الدفاع الإسرائيلي رصد محاولات تنظيم حزب الله الإرهابي إعادة بناء قدراته العسكرية وتعزيز تسليحه، ولن يسمح بأي خرق يشكّل تهديدًا لأمن دولة إسرائيل ومواطنيها. 🔸 لقد جرّ تنظيم حزب الله الإرهابي لبنان وسكانه إلى الحرب خدمةً لإيران خلال عملية "زئير الأسد"، وأطلق آلاف القذائف الصاروخية، بما في ذلك من مناطق تقع جنوب نهر الليطاني، حيث يُحظر وجود أي عناصر مسلحة أو منشآت عسكرية أو وسائل قتالية لا تتبع للحكومة اللبنانية أو لقوات الأمم المتحدة المؤقتة في لبنان (اليونيفيل).

Tampa and Fahmy's visit to southern Lebanon

An American official said the Lebanon-Israel talks in Tampa would “be conducted only between working teams on the security aspect of the framework agreement.”

Direct negotiations between Lebanon and Israel began in April, during the war, and produced a framework agreement in June. The agreement was intended to pave the way for Israel’s gradual withdrawal from occupied areas of southern Lebanon. But its implementation remains frozen, as the two sides have had no further contact since August.

Israeli legislative elections, during which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could be reelected, are scheduled for Oct. 27.

Meanwhile, Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy traveled Tuesday morning to Zawtar Gharbieh (Nabatieh), the first and only “pilot zone,” a few hundred meters from Israeli-occupied territory. Fahmy arrived by helicopter at the Zahrani base before heading to the village, our correspondent reported.

The Egyptian diplomat is touring southern Lebanon to assess conditions on the ground as part of the Arab League’s efforts to pursue a diplomatic solution and mobilize aid. He was accompanied by Lebanese Social Development Minister Haneen Sayed.

During a visit to the Church of the Annunciation, Fahmy said that “what is happening in southern Lebanon is unacceptable.”

“Arab efforts are underway to pressure Israel, which continues its illegal practices,” he added.

Lebanese Army accompanies farmers in the eastern sector

On the ground Tuesday morning, Israel launched a stun grenade and automatic weapons fire on Kfar Shuba (Hasbaya).

The incident came as the Lebanese Army said it had accompanied farmers from Rashaya al-Foukhar (Hasbaya) to their fields to secure the olive harvest. The Israeli army had prevented farmers in Kfar Shuba from reaching their olive fields, with orders and fire.

Israeli vehicles were also seen heading toward Zawtar Sharqieh in the Nabatieh district.

Two Israeli robotic tanks move north of Mansouri

Israel continued its attacks on south Lebanon overnight. Before midnight, two Israeli remote-controlled tanks reportedly left Mansouri (Sour) and headed north toward Aamrieh, south of a nearby Lebanese Army checkpoint. Mansouri marks the northernmost point of Israel's occupation along the coast.

The vehicles later withdrew to Bayada, in the occupied “buffer zone.” Israeli forces also fired artillery shells at Mansouri and the neighboring Zebqine Valley farther east.

Our correspondent also reported Israeli artillery fire on the outskirts of Mayfadoun and Kfar Tibnit (Nabatieh), as well as Beit Yahoun and Haddatha (Bint Jbeil) and Wadi Slouqi (Marjayoun).

In Khiam (Marjayoun), Israeli forces blew up several houses and fired medium-caliber automatic weapons at the town.

https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/10/19/israe.heading: Israel to resume commercial shipments to Gaza after Hamas fee dispute |  Cyprus Mail
https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/10/19/israe.body:
Israel said on Monday it would resume allowing commercial goods shipments into Gaza after a days-long halt over a tax dispute involving Hamas and merchants, restoring a key route for food and other essentials to the aid-dependent enclave.

COGAT, the Israeli military agency overseeing humanitarian affairs in Gaza, said it made the decision after merchants reported that Hamas authorities had withdrawn demands for payments of 10,000 shekels ($3,225) per truck.

“The resumption of coordination is being carried out in accordance with Israel’s commitment to the humanitarian provisions of the ceasefire agreement,” it said.

COGAT said the merchants’ accounts had not been independently verified and shipments would resume gradually, with priority given to essential goods ahead of winter.

Oversight would be tightened to ensure payments are made and received only through documented bank transfers, with any merchant found to have paid Hamas facing exclusion from the system.

Hamas said the 10,000-shekel fee was a voluntary contribution by better-off Gazans to a national fund supporting people in need in the war-ravaged territory.

Most Gazans remain dependent on aid after three years of war, repeated displacement and severe restrictions on aid deliveries. While last year’s US-brokered ceasefire halted the heaviest fighting, it has not ended Israeli attacks.

Local health officials said on Monday that at least five Palestinians, including a 14-year-old boy, were killed in separate Israeli strikes in Gaza City and Khan Younis. The Israeli military did not immediately comment.

Israel says Hamas has continued to rearm and carry out attacks in violation of the ceasefire, while Hamas accuses Israel of undermining the agreement.

Gaza health officials say about 1,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the October 2025 ceasefire, while Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza over the same period.

BEIRUT — Former Progressive Socialist Party (PSP) leader Walid Jumblatt warned Monday that Lebanon risks losing the South in the foreseeable future as Israeli attacks and the destruction of homes continue, saying the region would not return to what it was before even if Israeli forces withdraw.

In a program by local broadcaster LBC, Jumblatt said the South was not exclusively Shiite, stressing its diverse social fabric, and questioned why Lebanon should continue to serve as a battleground between Iran and Israel at the expense of the region.

"We cannot remain a battlefield for Iran to confront Israel, while losing what remains of the South," he said, arguing that the head of Hezbollah Naim Qassem "has no right to drag the country into wars that have nothing to do with us once again, and the losses will be enormous."

Jumblatt said the "destruction of homes had already changed the region" and "warned against further sacrifices," questioning the rationale for "dragging Lebanon into conflicts in which it has no direct stake."

He also criticized the Lebanese negotiating delegation, saying it had "miscalculated by assuming that signing the framework agreement would lead to an Israeli withdrawal."

"They thought that signing the tripartite framework agreement would bring about a withdrawal, but that did not happen," he said.

Read more In Iraq, Washington bets on integrating pro-Iranian militias into politics

He opposed "imposing preconditions that could pave the way for full normalization with Israel" and said he "did not support repealing the law criminalizing dealings with Israel. Does destruction mean peace? Does settlement-building mean peace?" he asked, questioning whether peace could be achieved with a country that did not want it.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in a phone call, earlier in October, to repeal Lebanon's 1955 Israel Boycott Law, arguing that the statute deters steps toward peace and diplomatic progress. Negotiations between Lebanon and Israel are set to resume in Tampa, Florida, following a nearly three-month suspension, and the Lebanese delegation is demanding an immediate end to the Israeli offensive and the full restoration of Lebanese sovereignty.

However, Israel has counter-asserted that it will maintain its military presence and occupation until Hezbollah is verified to be disarmed and its infrastructure dismantled. While Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy stated the negotiations enjoy full Arab support after meeting with President Joseph Aoun, the framework faces heavy domestic turbulence; Hezbollah and its parliamentary allies, including MP Hassan Fadlallah, strongly oppose the June 2026 agreement, warning that its strict enforcement risks sparking internal civil conflict.

Despite his criticism of the negotiations, Jumblatt called for "national dialogue to prevent further internal divisions amid wider regional tensions."

He said "Lebanon should maintain national unity and address domestic disagreements through dialogue, including with Hezbollah and Lebanese Forces (LF) leader Samir Geagea." He also called for talks with Iran, saying there was no alternative to dialogue.

Jumblatt warned that "neither Iran's regional policies nor those of the United States were serving Lebanon's interests, arguing that Israel was the only party benefiting from the wider confrontation."

Read more Lebanese-American lobby urges Washington to pressure Lebanon to repeal Israel boycott law

He also criticized what he described as attempts to drag Lebanon into wars unrelated to its interests, warning that the consequences would be severe for the country and its population. "Why sacrifice the South and the children of the South, both Shiite and Christian, and push some Druze into Israel's arms?" he asked, according to LBC.

Jumblatt further called for support for the Lebanese Army, condemning campaigns targeting its commander and saying strengthening the institution should begin with improving military personnel's salaries. He also urged the government to establish clear priorities, citing rising living costs and the risk of social unrest, and welcomed Qatari promises of support for the electricity sector.

On Friday, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam announced that Qatar will finance, implement and operate a project in Lebanon’s electricity sector without requiring an upfront investment from the Lebanese Treasury.

Jumblatt concluded by reiterating the need for dialogue across political divides, arguing that "Lebanon could protect itself amid regional power struggles only by addressing its internal disputes."

LONDON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Britain will fly Royal Air Force ​Typhoon fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect ‌Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure from Houthi aerial attacks, the Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday.

The ministry said the aircraft would operate ​only in a defensive role and would not conduct ​offensive strikes against the Iran-aligned Houthis, whose attacks ⁠Britain says threaten regional stability and risk disrupting energy supplies ​and trade routes.

"The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ​ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate ​the situation in the region," defence minister Wes Streeting ​said in a statement.

"That’s why today I have approved further UK military ‌support. ⁠RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles."

The additional support follows a request from Saudi Arabia's government, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier ​this month ​Britain was prepared ⁠to consider.

Britain will also deploy an Atlas A400M transport aircraft and military advisers, expanding assistance announced ​in September which included an RAF Voyager air-to-air ​refuelling ⁠aircraft but not fighter jets.

Houthi attacks against Saudi oil facilities and other infrastructure have intensified in recent weeks as the conflict in ⁠Yemen ​has escalated.

Inside Yemen, authorities said a ​Houthi strike on Monday against a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces killed ​58 people.

https://www.dailysabah.com/politics/dipl.heading: Türkiye indispensable to European security, Belgium FM says | Daily Sabah
https://www.dailysabah.com/politics/dipl.body:
Belgium emphasized Türkiye's strategic importance to European security Tuesday as senior ministers from both countries met in Brussels, reviving high-level bilateral dialogue after a decadelong hiatus.

Seven Belgian and Turkish ministers gathered at Egmont Palace to strengthen cooperation on security, justice, migration and economic relations.

The Turkish delegation included Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek and Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi, while Belgium was represented by Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot and senior ministers responsible for justice, security and migration.

The Belgian Foreign Ministry described Türkiye as a crucial strategic partner, citing its NATO membership, role in Black Sea security and diplomatic engagement with both Russia and Ukraine.

"You cannot seriously discuss European security without engaging with Türkiye," Prevot said, highlighting Ankara's influence in regions vital to European stability.

He also pointed to Türkiye's diplomatic efforts in the Middle East, particularly Gaza and Syria, as well as the Horn of Africa.

Counterterrorism and organized crime dominated discussions, with both sides working toward a bilateral police cooperation action plan aimed at strengthening coordination between law enforcement agencies.

The proposed agreement would facilitate faster intelligence-sharing, joint training and exchanges of expertise to tackle cross-border criminal networks.

Belgian Security and Home Affairs Minister Bernard Quintin stressed that closer cooperation was essential as organized crime increasingly operated across national borders.

The ministers also discussed strengthening judicial cooperation while maintaining respect for the rule of law and fundamental legal safeguards.

Migration management emerged as another priority, with officials exploring closer coordination on migration policies and consular affairs.

Belgian Asylum and Migration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt described Türkiye as an important partner for Belgium and the European Union, emphasizing that effective migration management required cooperation beyond EU borders.

Beyond security and migration, Belgium expressed interest in expanding bilateral ties in defense, energy, industry, innovation and trade.

The talks marked the resumption of a high-level diplomatic mechanism that had remained inactive for 10 years, underscoring both countries' efforts to deepen cooperation amid evolving European and regional security challenges.

https://www.kurdistan24.net/en/story/947.heading: PKK Official Presses Ankara for Next Steps in Peace Process
https://www.kurdistan24.net/en/story/947.body:
PKK official Duran Kalkan says Türkiye's peace process remains largely rhetorical and calls for action on Öcalan's status and a legal political framework.

ERBIL (Kurdistan24) - A senior PKK figure has accused Ankara of delaying Türkiye's peace process, saying the group has withdrawn its armed forces from inside the country while the Turkish government has yet to take what he considers substantive political and legal steps in return.

Duran Kalkan, a member of the Abdullah Öcalan Academy of Social Sciences, told a channel close to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) that the group had taken what he described as "fundamental and historic" steps toward the peace and democratic society process.

Kalkan said Ankara, by contrast, had largely kept the process at the level of public statements.

He argued that despite the period that has passed since initiatives aimed at dissolving the PKK began, no decision has been made regarding the status and conditions of imprisoned PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan.

Kalkan also claimed that throughout 2025 and 2026 the PKK withdrew its armed forces from Türkiye and neighboring areas, and said the organization currently poses no armed threat to Türkiye's security.

His remarks represent the PKK's assessment of the process.

Kalkan said further implementation of the decisions adopted at the PKK's 12th Congress would require what he called Öcalan's "physical freedom," together with a legal and political framework allowing former members of the organization to participate in democratic politics.

He also warned Turkish authorities against concluding that the state no longer needs engagement with the other side because of the PKK's disarmament decisions.

According to Kalkan, calls for the organization to "completely lay down its arms" no longer reflect conditions on the ground because, in his account, armed forces capable of threatening Türkiye have already been withdrawn.

He characterized continuing demands for disarmament as an attempt to maintain pressure on the PKK and delay implementation of other parts of the process.

Kalkan further accused Turkish authorities of linking the initiative too closely to domestic political calculations and elections, arguing that this had slowed genuine progress.

The current process traces back to late 2024, when Nationalist Movement Party leader Devlet Bahçeli called on Öcalan to address parliament and urge the PKK to dissolve.

On Feb. 27, 2025, Öcalan called on the organization to convene a congress, lay down its weapons and dissolve itself.

The PKK subsequently held its 12th Congress in May 2025 and announced a decision to dissolve the organization and disarm.

Türkiye has also taken steps during the process.

In August 2026, the Turkish Parliament approved a limited amnesty measure covering disarmed PKK members. An oversight committee chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz was also established to monitor implementation.

Kalkan, however, argued that those developments have not addressed what the PKK regards as the central political and legal requirements of the process, particularly Öcalan's status and a framework for democratic participation.

His comments therefore highlight the gap between steps already taken and the further measures sought by the PKK side.

The process has moved considerably from the initial political opening in late 2024 through Öcalan's disarmament appeal and the PKK's subsequent congress decisions.

For Kalkan, however, its next stage depends on Ankara moving beyond declarations and existing limited measures toward decisions on Öcalan and the political future of former PKK members.

He said the organization would continue pressing for those changes as conditions for fully implementing the remaining decisions of its 12th Congress.

Kurdistan24 correspondent Ebidulselam Tûtincî contributed to this report.

https://turkishminute.com/2026/10/19/erd.heading: Erdoğan says Turkey shut or took over Gülen-linked schools in over 50 countries, vows to press on - Turkish Minute
https://turkishminute.com/2026/10/19/erd.body:
Turkey has secured the closure or takeover of schools linked to the faith-based Gülen movement in more than 50 countries, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said on Thursday, vowing to continue his government’s campaign against the group abroad.

Speaking at an event in Ankara marking the 10th anniversary of the state-run Turkish Maarif Foundation (TMV), Erdoğan praised the foundation’s takeover of schools previously associated with the movement and credited the Foreign Ministry, the foundation and other government institutions with carrying out the campaign abroad. He said the campaign had intensified after a July 2016 coup attempt.

Erdoğan also described the Gülen movement as a “network of treachery” and its schools “dens of sedition,” saying its supporters would become “much more pitiable, much more wretched.” The remarks reflect a longstanding pattern of hate speech, with Erdoğan and other government officials portraying the movement’s followers as internal enemies and using dehumanizing language to legitimize their persecution, while pro-government media have amplified the rhetoric.

Erdoğan has targeted the faith-based Gülen movement, inspired by Muslim cleric Fethullah Gülen, who died in 2024, since corruption investigations in December 2013 implicated Erdoğan as well as some members of his family and inner circle. He dismissed the probes as a Gülenist conspiracy and designated the movement as a terrorist organization in May 2016, intensifying a sweeping crackdown after the coup attempt in July of the same year that he accused Gülen of orchestrating. The movement denies involvement in the attempted coup or any terrorist activity.

Erdoğan did not identify the countries involved, specify how many schools were affected or say where closures had been complete or partial.

A July 2026 report by the human rights group Solidarity with Others documented the closure, confiscation or transfer of at least 162 Gülen-linked educational institutions in 29 countries, based on data compiled through March 2023. Of those, 131 were taken over directly by the Turkish Maarif Foundation. The report estimated that approximately 7,800 employees were affected.

Since the July 2016 coup attempt, Ankara has pressed foreign governments to close or transfer Gülen-linked schools to the TMV, part of a broader campaign against perceived opponents abroad that human rights organizations have described as transnational repression.

The foundation is the only organization other than Turkey’s Education Ministry authorized to open schools overseas on behalf of the Turkish state.

The campaign has also extended beyond school closures and takeovers to the educators themselves. SCF has documented cases of educators associated with the Gülen movement being abducted or forcibly returned to Turkey from countries including Kosovo, Pakistan, Malaysia and Myanmar. Many Turkish teachers at schools targeted for takeover fled their host countries, fearing arrest or extradition, and sought refuge in Europe, the United States or Canada.

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) cited Freedom House data listing Turkey among the world’s 10 leading perpetrators of physical transnational repression in a June resolution. The rights group documented 160 such incidents attributed to Turkey from 2014 through 2025.

This article is republished from the Stockholm Center for Freedom.

White House envoy Steve Witkoff is traveling to Oslo for talks Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders, a U.S. official said.

The big picture: The talks will bring together Ukraine, European allies and the U.S. as they seek to develop a peace proposal to present to Russia.

- The Oslo talks are expected to include Zelensky, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO.

Driving the news: The U.S. official said that following Oslo, Witkoff is also planning to travel to Russia, where he hopes to meet with President Vladimir Putin and present ideas developed in close consultation with Ukraine and European partners.

- Trump adviser Jared Kushner has the flu and will not attend the Oslo meeting in person, but will participate virtually, the U.S. official said.

- The planned meetings in Oslo build on the discussions held at Witkoff's Miami-area Shell Bay club, where Zelensky committed to reviewing and advancing a series of proposals aimed at creating a pathway toward a comprehensive and durable peace agreement, the U.S. official added.

Zoom in: The U.S. official said American, Ukrainian and European representatives worked together over the past week to develop the proposals.

- "Steve and Jared also spoke with President Zelensky on Sunday to review progress and discuss next steps," the U.S. official said.

- The trip is also expected to include efforts to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher whom the U.S. says has been wrongfully detained in Russia.

What's next: The U.S. official said the discussions are focused on two parallel tracks:

1. Securing Ukraine's future: Establishing a sovereign, secure, and prosperous future for Ukraine, including credible security guarantees, European integration, and a comprehensive postwar economic framework that addresses Ukraine's financial needs and creates opportunities for long-term growth and investment.

2. Creating the conditions for a durable peace: Developing a comprehensive proposal to Russia that addresses the issues necessary to end the war, establishes a new and enduring security architecture between Russia and Europe, and explores opportunities for postwar economic cooperation.

- "President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia," the U.S. official said.

- "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump's objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."

WASHINGTON — In an unprecedented move, A Russian government-owned satellite spent weeks stalking an ICEYE satellite widely believed to be providing synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery to Ukraine — coming as close as 500 meters (about a third of a mile), according to space watching firm LeoLabs.

In a press release today, LeoLabs said Russia’s Cosmos 2612 “conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers toward ICEYE-X36” between Oct. 15-19 that involved “continued maneuvering around ICEYE-X36, shifting between positions ahead of and behind the commercial satellite.”

While Russia’s Cosmos birds have previously been observed closely following other Western satellites, Adam Marsh, LeoLabs vice president for technical solutions, told Breaking Defense that this was a first-of-its-kind rendezvous and proximity operation (RPO).

“This is the most advanced and potentially dangerous uncooperative RPO we’ve observed,” he said.

Victoria Samson, chief director of Space Security and Stability for Secure World Foundation, agreed.

“What is new is that I don’t think that there has ever been an uncoordinated RPO that was close,” she told Breaking Defense. “Also, in these earlier cases, the satellite that was being approached was a USG satellite; obviously in this case, it was a commercial satellite.”

LeoLabs’ analysis concluded that Cosmos 2612 “demonstrated a sequence of capabilities that could be used to inspect, characterize, shadow, or potentially interfere with another spacecraft. The observed tactics included:

A commitment to long-term operational value.

According to a blog post by longtime space watcher Marco Langbroek, the Cosmos 2612 ― which was launched in April ― began its “worrisome” stalking mission Sept. 30 and subsequently undertook a series of maneuvers “clearly designed” to catch up to the ICEYE satellite.

Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said in a web post on Friday that Cosmos 2612’s maneuvers should be viewed as a likely threat, given that the ICEYE satellite “supports Ukraine” in its effort to repel Russia’s 2022 invasion.

“Given Russia’s history of testing on-orbit weapons, policymakers should assume Cosmos 2612 could take an action that threatens the commercial satellite,” he wrote. “But the risk extends beyond just one satellite. A Russian counterspace activity in the vicinity of Western satellites should be assessed within the context of aggressive Russian gray zone activities targeting U.S. and European interests.”

ICEYE, headquartered in Finland, first announced an agreement with Ukraine to provide SAR imagery via a dedicated satellite in 2022, but has never publicly identified which specific satellite was provided.

Samson noted that although ICEYE-X36 may be collecting data used by Ukraine, although that has not been publicly confirmed. The spacecraft is operated by it’s US arm, ICEYE US, and was launched from the United States in 2024. That makes ICEYE-X36 a US satellite — or at least one for which the United States is the launching state, she explained.

“Russia and the US aren’t at war with each other, knock wood, but this does make me wonder why the USG [US government] has been silent on this matter,” she added.
