The implementation of the North–South transport corridor project was at the center of the Russian-Iranian talks that took place on October 19 in Dushanbe. The Russian side is waiting for Tehran to document the purchase of land for the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway section. At the same time, in the open part of the negotiations, the parties did not ignore the conflict between Tehran and Washington, which could turn into a war again at any moment. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, who arrived in Tajikistan to participate in SCO events, recalled that Moscow immediately condemned the actions of the United States and provided humanitarian support to the Islamic Republic.

Mikhail Mishustin is in Dushanbe to attend a meeting of the Council of Heads of Government of the SCO member states scheduled for October 20. The day before, immediately after landing at the international airport of the capital of Tajikistan, Mishustin went to bilateral talks with Iranian Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref.

Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin arrives at Dushanbe International Airport

The meeting took place in one of the cottages of the hotel complex owned by the executive office of the President of Tajikistan. This is a closed area, where high-ranking delegations arriving in Dushanbe often live. The atmosphere is impressive: the buildings have parquet floors with intricate patterns, coffered ceilings, and fountains and perfect cleanliness greet guests on the street. Right before the start of the events, local staff actively cleaned the red carpet.

The only thing missing here were peacocks. At least, it was them, and not the members of the delegations, that the journalists were looking for at first. The organizers promised that exotic birds will definitely be available tomorrow, during the main events of the SCO summit.

The fact that the agenda of the negotiations covers a wide variety of areas, from diplomacy to trade, was also indicated by the composition of the participants. The Russian delegation included representatives of several departments at once: Maxim Reshetnikov, Head of the Ministry of Economic Development, Andrey Rudenko, Deputy Head of the Russian Foreign Ministry, as well as deputy ministers of Industry, Agriculture and Energy. The Iranian delegation was also representative.

Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref during a meeting in Dushanbe, where a meeting of the Council of Heads of Government of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization member states will be held.

The atmosphere was positive even before the start of the negotiations. Mikhail Mishustin began the conversation with a polite gesture, conveying to Aref greetings from himself and Vladimir Putin for Iranian President Masoud Peseshkian. Most recently, the leaders of the two countries met in Turkmenistan, where the CIS summit was held. Mikhail Mishustin generally noted the positive trajectory of bilateral relations: trade between the two countries is growing, including thanks to the free trade zone of Iran with the EAEU.

Meanwhile, the most difficult point was the linguistic nuances: the translation from Farsi into Russian turned out to be so specific that it was clear from the expressions on the faces of the correspondents and even some participants in the negotiations that not everything was clear. And after the end of the official part, during a conversation between the press and Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk, it became clear that the Iranian translator could not accurately convey the entire content of the introductory speech.

It remains to be hoped that the translation for the Iranian side was more accurate, because really important issues were discussed — first of all, the development of the North–South corridor. According to Alexey Overchuk, Tehran has already notified Russia that the land for the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway section has been fully purchased. Moscow is now waiting for documentary confirmation of this step, the Deputy Prime Minister stressed. This is the last element of the North–South overland route, without which the corridor cannot be fully operational.

Russian Minister of Transport Vitaly Saveliev and Iranian Minister of Roads and Urban Development Mehrdad Bazrpash (center, from left to right) during the signing ceremony of the Russian-Iranian cooperation agreement on the creation of the Rasht-Astara railway in Iran, May 17, 2023.

According to orientalist Roland Bijamov, Russia and Iran are connected by geography, and the current situation in the international arena simply leaves them no choice but to move closer. The expert notes that negotiations are currently underway in the energy sector: Gazprom and the Iranian National Gas Company (NIGC) The route of the future pipeline for Russian gas supplies and the pricing mechanisms are being agreed upon. In addition, Russian investments in the development of Iranian oil fields are on the agenda. Another important area is the Bushehr NPP. Construction work on the site has been suspended due to the Middle East escalation, but Bijamov is confident that the project will be implemented.

The unresolved conflict between Iran and the United States has not been left out. Mikhail Mishustin recalled that Russia condemned the armed aggression against Iran and provided large-scale humanitarian assistance, including supplies of medicines and medical products.

At the same time, the talks in Dushanbe took place against the background of the risk of a new escalation in the Middle East. Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran Ali Rezaei announced the development of a new defense plan in case of external aggression. According to him, his country's response this time will be bigger than during previous conflicts. Iran's new defense minister, Mehrdad Ehlaqi, however, believes that the United States would not dare to attack Iran, as in this case it would suffer great damage itself.

But the American media does not rule out a scenario with direct military intervention by Washington. According to CNN, the American command is exploring the possibility of using the largest non-nuclear munition in the US arsenal, and the main targets in the event of an attack could be Iran's nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure.

US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to media reports, discussed possible scenarios for new attacks on Iran ahead of the parliamentary elections in Israel on October 27 and the midterm elections to the US Congress on November 3.

Although Trump has promised not to attack Iran until after the congressional elections, the history of the confrontation with Tehran proves that the rhetoric of the White House often serves only as a screen for preparing real strikes. In the past, Washington has repeatedly used diplomatic pauses to lull the enemy's vigilance.

Shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most pressing issues in relations between Iran and the United States. At the end of September, Tehran handed over to the United States through Qatar a seven-day plan to restore the operation of this artery. At a meeting with the Russian Prime Minister, Mohammad Reza Aref said that Iran understands the concerns of its partners regarding Hormuz. But all the consequences, according to him, arose because of the actions of the United States.

Araqchi previously clarified that the steps that Washington should take have already been fixed in the interim memorandum of understanding and cessation of hostilities. The parties signed it remotely in mid-June with the mediation of third countries. That document, in particular, obliged Iran to waive fees from merchant ships for passage in exchange for the lifting of all sanctions.

Strikes before the midterm elections in the United States are unlikely, but their holding in late autumn or in the new year is quite expected, says Farhad Ibragimov, a lecturer at the RUDN University Faculty of Economics and an expert at the Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation. Now, in his opinion, the Pentagon is developing plans for an active military campaign against Iran, working on mistakes and testing the ground — the return of American aircraft carriers to the Middle East is not just happening.

At the same time, Farhad Ibragimov drew attention to the current position of Donald Trump regarding the Russian Federation, anti-Russian sanctions and Ukraine. The statements and agreements that are causing fury in Brussels and Kiev may indicate that the White House is counting on Moscow's help in resolving the Iranian crisis. According to him, it is Russia, not China or regional players like Pakistan and Oman, that has the closest ties and coordination with Iran.

Moscow has previously stated its readiness to provide mediation services to resolve the situation between the United States and Iran. Moscow has relevant experience: during the Vienna negotiations on the restoration of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) in 2021-2022, the Russian delegation repeatedly helped Western countries and Iran find a common language.

For Russia, normalization of the situation in the Middle East is important for several reasons. Moscow is actively cooperating not only with Iran, but also with other Middle Eastern monarchies, which, in the event of an escalation, will inevitably be drawn into the conflict. First of all, we are talking about the UAE and Saudi Arabia, whose partnership determines the stability of the entire global energy market. In addition, any large-scale logistical disruption due to the escalation around Iran could paralyze the operation of the Caspian route and block access to the Persian Gulf.

https://www.voanews.com/a/china-philippi.heading: China-Philippines War of Words Raises South China Sea Tensions
https://www.voanews.com/a/china-philippi.body:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The Philippines has summoned China’s ambassador to protest remarks suggesting Beijing could easily defeat Manila in a conflict, escalating a diplomatic dispute amid tensions over the South China Sea.

Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro told Ambassador Jing Quan on Monday that his remarks were “provocative and unacceptable” and risked worsening bilateral relations.

China defended Jing. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning urged the Philippines to “rein in the irresponsible words and actions of individual politicians,” accusing some Philippine officials of exaggerating the issue.

The dispute began last Thursday when Jing responded to reporters’ questions about Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.’s description of China as a regional “troublemaker.”

Jing said the Philippines should be grateful to have a neighbor like China, adding “if we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force and we love peace.”

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said last Friday that the remarks sounded “very much like a threat” and called for an explanation from the Chinese envoy.

The exchange comes as competing claims in the South China Sea continue to strain relations and tests U.S. security commitments to the Philippines.

The South China Sea is a major international shipping route with rich fishing grounds, potential energy resources and strategic importance.China claims most of the waterway, while the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan also have claims.

In 2016, an international arbitration tribunal rejected key elements of China’s broad claims to historic rights in the sea. The tribunal also found that China had violated the Philippines’ sovereign rights in parts of its exclusive economic zone. Beijing has rejected the ruling.

For the Philippines, the dispute affects fishing, maritime law enforcement, resource development and its ability to exercise its claimed rights in the waters.

No direct military-to-military communication

Recent incidents in the South China Sea have added to tensions.

On September 27, China held joint naval and air exercises near the disputed Scarborough Shoal, known in China as Huangyan Dao and in the Philippines as Bajo de Masinloc. The Philippines and the United States criticized the exercises.

On October 4, the Philippine Coast Guard said Chinese vessels obstructed a law enforcement operation involving a foreign fishing boat suspected of dynamite fishing near Thitu Island, known in the Philippines as Pag-asa Island.

On October 8, Manila accused Chinese coast guard vessels of using water cannons and obstructing the evacuation of a sick Philippine Navy servicemember near Second Thomas Shoal, delaying the operation by nearly 10 hours.

On October 15, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. reiterated that the military communications between the two countries remain suspended for security reasons. He accused Beijing of misusing the channels and distorting conversations.

The direct military-to-military communication between Beijing and Manila was put on hold in 2023. Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan warned that a failure to restore military communications could increase the risk of confrontation.

The dispute also has implications for Washington. The United States and the Philippines are bound by a mutual defense treaty, which covers armed attacks on Philippine armed forces, aircraft and public vessels in the South China Sea.

Manila has also strengthened security cooperation with Japan and Australia.Washington faces the challenge of supporting its ally while deterring aggression and avoiding a wider military conflict. The suspension of military communications between China and the Philippines has raised concerns that poor communication during maritime confrontations could lead to miscalculation.

BEIJING/TAIPEI, Oct 20 (Reuters) - China's military said on Tuesday it had sent forces to watch a US warship that "illegally" entered waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, while further north in the waterway, Taiwan reported a standoff with a Chinese vessel.

China views almost all of the South China Sea as its own territory, despite overlapping claims by Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam, with recent tension most pronounced between Beijing and Manila.

The Chinese military's Southern Theatre Command said the USS Charleston "illegally intruded" into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands without Chinese government approval in the early hours of Tuesday.

"The US action infringes upon China's sovereign rights and interests, jeopardises maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability," it said in a statement.

"The US side should immediately cease such activities."

China's navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the ship, it added.

The US Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It generally refers to such missions as "freedom of navigation operations", though its last known one in the South China Sea was more than a year ago.

A Philippines' military spokesperson said the US ship "did not trespass into 'Chinese territory'," adding that no nation had the authority to require prior permission for "lawful transit through international waters."

Last month, a China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine boat on a refuelling mission near the same shoal, according to the Philippine Coast Guard. China blamed the collision on the Philippine side.

China and the Philippines, which has a mutual defence treaty with the US, both contest sovereignty over Sabina Shoal and the entire Spratly Islands archipelago.

In a separate incident on Tuesday at the top end of the South China Sea, Taiwan's Coast Guard said a Chinese Coast Guard ship had entered restricted waters near the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands.

The Taiwan Coast Guard said its ship the "Taichung" was dispatched to warn away the Chinese boat, while both sides broadcast messages to each other.

The Chinese ship broadcast that "the so-called Republic of China does not exist", referring to Taiwan's official name, while the Taiwanese ship broadcast back that "the Republic of China, Taiwan, is a sovereign and independent country", Taiwan's Coast Guard said, adding the standoff was continuing.

China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The office said last week that Taiwan must "bear the consequences" of its Coast Guard using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas.

The Pratas Islands lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong, but are only lightly defended and security is the responsibility of Taiwan's Coast Guard.

China has also been stepping up coast guard activity around Taiwan, including off the island's east coast, causing concern in Western capitals.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory.

Speaking at a forum in Taipei on Tuesday, the chair of a review commission appointed by the US Congress said Chinese coast guard patrols to the east of Taiwan were "highly destabilising".

Addressing the same event, Taiwan's National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu said China had no legal claim to the waters off the island's east.

German Air Force aircraft escorted the Mongolian President’s plane from the moment it entered German airspace. Following its landing, the aircraft received a ceremonial fly-past. An honor guard of the German Armed Forces also paid tribute to the President, accompanied by a 21-gun salute.

They will also sign the “Joint Declaration between Mongolia and the Federal Republic of Germany” and identify priority areas to strengthen further and expand their strategic partnership.

The two Presidents will inaugurate the exhibition “Chinggis Khaan and the World of the Mongols” in Berlin. Mongolia and Germany established diplomatic relations on January 31, 1974, and elevated their ties to a Comprehensive Partnership in 2008. During President Steinmeier’s state visit to Mongolia in 2024, marking the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations, the two countries upgraded their relationship to a Strategic Partnership.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to arrive in Türkiye on a trip expected to give a new push to relations between the two countries that are working toward a free trade agreement (FTA).

Carney will travel ​to Ankara and Istanbul from Wednesday to Friday and is scheduled to hold talks with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan during what will mark the first dedicated bilateral visit to NATO ally Türkiye by a Canadian leader.

The trip marks Carney's latest diplomatic effort as he seeks to reduce the country's ⁠reliance on the United States, by far its biggest trading ​partner, after a collapse in trade talks in August.

The talks with Erdoğan are meant to cover political and diplomatic issues as well as trade, defense industry, energy and mutual investment.

Carney and his delegation are also expected to meet Turkish business representatives to discuss opportunities in areas such as aviation, advanced technologies and critical minerals.

The premier has ⁠vowed to double Canada's non-U.S. trade over the next decade and has rushed to establish ties ​with a host of countries, including China and ​India, ⁠with which it had past strains.

Relations received a boost from the NATO leaders' summit in Ankara in July, when Carney and Erdoğan formally launched negotiations for a free trade agreement.

Türkiye has also agreed to join Canada's ​Defense Security and Resilience Bank as one of 10 founding member nations of ​Carney's multilateral "middle powers" bank.

The bank's purpose ​is to bolster ⁠the defense of like-minded allied ⁠nations by raising up to 100 billion pounds ($134 ⁠billion) ​in cheap financing.

The two countries' technical teams have worked intensively since July to define the scope and goals of the trade agreement.

Trade Minister Ömer Bolat and Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu also met in June to discuss advancing the economic partnership. They described energy as a "promising area" for deeper cooperation, and discussed possible cooperation in nuclear energy.

Türkiye's exports to Canada last year totaled about $1.58 billion, and its imports from Canada about $1.16 billion. That put two-way trade at about $2.74 billion.

The leading Turkish exports in 2025 were boilers, machinery and mechanical appliances, at $158.8 million, followed by iron and steel at $104.4 million and articles of iron or steel at $97.0 million.

In the first eight months of this year, exports to Canada reached about $1.02 billion and imports about $955 million, bringing trade close to $2 billion.

Boilers and machinery again led exports at $96.1 million, followed by aluminum and aluminum articles at $73.8 million and edible fruits and nuts at $49.5 million.

If an FTA is signed, the two countries aim to lift trade to $7-$8 billion in the short term, and to $10 billion later.

Visitors from Canada to Türkiye rose 6.1% to 321,271 in 2025, from 302,728 in 2024. In the first eight months of 2026, arrivals rose 2.9% year-over-year to 209,176.

According to Statistics Canada, Canada's stock of direct investment in Türkiye stood at CA$3.3 billion ($2.35 billion) as of 2025. Türkiye's direct investment stock in Canada was CA$233 million.

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process towards independence, delivering a victory for the prime minister, Mark Carney, and supporters of Canadian unity.

With more than 1.5m votes counted, 76% supported remaining in Canada, while close to 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.

Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, Alberta’s capital, said: “Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.

Alberta’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours, but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.

In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.

Carney warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government. “A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.

The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.

Smith’s tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months she has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.

The referendum became a political liability for Smith’s party, whose popular support has tumbled in recent months, including with the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold in a byelection.

Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, said the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city”, amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.

“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” Farkas said. “And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together, because no result will permanently put this to bed. “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

https://english.news.cn/20261019/ff2ed29.heading: Fire at Canadian military base kills four, injures 39
https://english.news.cn/20261019/ff2ed29.body:
A military training exercise in #Alberta, Canada, turned deadly when a fast-moving wildfire swept through troops conducting live-fire drills.

Four soldiers were killed and 39 others injured, including 19 critically.

Military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained enough for training to continue.

But then the wind shifted. The flames raced 1 km in just 36 seconds.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called it one of Canada's worst peacetime military tragedies on home soil, ordering flags lowered on federal buildings nationwide.

By Juliane Rodust and Johannes Neudecker, dpa

US President Donald Trump has expressed openness to a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss nuclear disarmament.

"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," Trump told reporters on Monday when asked about the possibility of such a meeting.

A meeting between the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers to discuss disarmament would be "a very positive thing for the world," Trump said, adding that he would be willing to pursue it at any time.

He said he would also raise other issues, like the war in Ukraine, during such talks.

A meeting with Putin and Xi could take place in November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

The Washington Post reported that Putin had proposed the idea.

China has not confirmed plans for such a meeting. Asked about Trump's remarks, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Tuesday that she had no information to share at present.

Trump has been sharpening his rhetoric towards Ukraine, accusing the country of ingratitude and of failing to offer anything in return for US support as it continues to defend itself against Russia's full-scale invasion launched in February 2022.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has in turn accused Trump of adopting a position favourable to the Kremlin and scaling back US defence and intelligence support for his country.

In his Monday remarks, Trump said Russia "has been fine on Ukraine" and "hasn't been doing much."

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha meanwhile warned that a trilateral meeting between Russia, China and the US without Ukraine's participation would only "encourage" Moscow to continue its war, as Russia steps up round-the-clock attacks using jet-powered drones and Ukraine's air defences grow increasingly depleted.

Putin did not deserve a seat at the negotiating table, Sybiha wrote on X on Monday.

"Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandizement and give him a stature he does not deserve. He is not a global leader; he is a war criminal," he said.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 19 (Yonhap) -- U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday expressed uncertainty about the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in China next month, saying he was not sure whether anyone had requested such a meeting.

Trump made the remarks when asked by a reporter whether he expected to secure a meeting with Kim during his planned attendance at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen.

"Oh, I don't know. I don't know," Trump said at the White House. "I'm not sure that anybody's asking for a meeting."

The president nevertheless emphasized his personal ties with the North Korean leader. "I get along with him very well," Trump said. "But my relationship with Kim Jong-un is very good."

In August, Trump said that he hoped to meet Kim later this year, adding to speculation that he might seek to rekindle his personal diplomacy with Kim that led to three bilateral in-person meetings: the first in Singapore in June 2018, the second in Hanoi in February 2019 and the third at the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom.

Last Monday, Trump said that he may meet Kim during his upcoming trip to Asia, adding, "That'll be exciting, won't it? But I get along with him."

Tommy Pigott, spokesperson for the State Department, said earlier that Trump does not view talks with North Korea as a "concession" and is willing to engage Pyongyang if doing so serves U.S. national interests.

https://www.rferl.org/a/rubio-central-as.heading: Rubio Trip Highlights US Push For Deeper Ties With Central Asia
https://www.rferl.org/a/rubio-central-as.body:
SAMARKAND, Uzbekistan -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed Uzbekistan on October 20 for India after meetings with all five Central Asian countries, wrapping up a visit aimed at expanding Washington’s economic and diplomatic engagement with a region increasingly intent on shaping its own international partnerships.

Rubio’s visit to the historic Silk Road city of Samarkand brought together the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. He also met Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoev and attended a US-Uzbekistan business council event alongside a delegation of nearly 300 American business leaders.

The visit produced several concrete initiatives, including Uzbekistan’s signing of the US-led Artemis Accords on peaceful space exploration and a bilateral investment agreement that the parties said would total $12 billion when implemented.

But the broader significance of Rubio’s trip may lie less in the immediate announcements than in Washington’s renewed attention to Central Asia -- and its stated willingness to pursue closer ties without demanding that regional governments choose between the US, Russia, and China.

“This is not simply a contest between outside powers,” US Ambassador to Uzbekistan Jonathan Henick told RFE/RL in an interview as Rubio departed Samarkand.

Henick said Central Asian countries had demonstrated their independence and their ability to determine the terms of their own international relationships over the 35 years since the collapse of the Soviet Union.

The United States, he said, wants to offer them additional options, both politically and economically, that would help them preserve their independence and expand their room for maneuver.

Henick said Rubio’s visit represented a historic expansion of American engagement, with growing economic and commercial ties accompanying closer political contacts.

But he also stressed that American interests were coinciding with changes already underway in Central Asia, rather than creating them from scratch.

Uzbekistan, he said, was in the midst of a historic period of economic reform under Mirziyoev, whose government has sought to create a more business-friendly environment and attract foreign investment.

“The coincidence of the attention from Washington with the opportunities that we’re seeing here,” Henick said, was helping drive the transformation.

Luke Coffey, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, offered a more measured assessment of the immediate diplomatic results.

Speaking to RFE/RL, Coffey described Rubio’s visit as largely a maintenance exercise intended to keep agreements reached during last year’s White House summit on track.

He considered that earlier gathering more consequential than the Samarkand meetings themselves.

Nevertheless, he said, the Trump administration’s broader actions during its second term had collectively returned Central Asia to Washington’s strategic map -- a development he welcomed.

All five Central Asian states retain significant commercial and diplomatic links with Russia, while China remains a major regional economic power. Their relationships with Iran also vary.

Rubio acknowledged that reality during his visit, saying countries wanted as many international relationships as possible. Uzbekistan, he noted, had made clear that it wanted to be friends with everybody.

The question of whether Washington can expand its influence without pressuring Central Asian governments to distance themselves from Russia and China emerged as a central theme of the visit.

Henick rejected the notion that the region should be viewed primarily through the lens of competition among outside powers.

“For too long we’ve been characterizing this region as, you know, as sometimes they call it the Great Game,” he said. “It’s outside powers competing in the region. Honestly, I think that completely mischaracterizes what’s happening here.”

Coffey agreed that the US should not seek to force regional governments to choose Washington over Moscow or Beijing.

Geography, economic ties, history, and cultural connections make such a choice unrealistic, he said. Instead, Washington should remain actively engaged and help its partners balance their relationships with major powers.

Angela Howard, a research analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Center on Economic and Financial Power, said Rubio’s approach could make it easier for Washington to establish partnerships that might otherwise be blocked by an insistence on choosing sides.

The administration is signaling that it is interested in the region, prepared to compete with Russia and China, and prioritizing economic statecraft, Howard said.

An approach that avoids an “us-versus-them” framework could allow the United States to provide alternatives to Russia, China, and Iran incrementally, she added.

Howard argued that Washington would make more progress in limiting its competitors’ influence by pursuing specific policy changes -- including action against sanctions-evasion networks -- than by issuing ultimatums that Central Asian governments would be unlikely to accept.

The visit’s economic agenda was underscored by the large business delegation accompanying Rubio, as the administration seeks greater access to Central Asia’s markets and natural resources, including critical minerals.

During his visit, Rubio defended the commercial dimension of American diplomacy, saying the United States wanted fair competition and an opportunity for its companies.

At a business council event, he also argued that US foreign policy should not focus so heavily on immediate crises that it neglects long-term opportunities.

“Our focus on a problem region or a problem country or a problem issue in the world still has to be there, but it cannot come at the expense of embracing opportunities,” Rubio said. “You have to be able to do both.”

Henick said the visit had helped businesses already working on deals make progress in their relationships and introduced other American companies to opportunities in Uzbekistan for the first time. He expected many of those first-time visitors to return.

Uzbekistan’s signature on the Artemis Accords could also open new avenues for cooperation in space exploration, the ambassador said.

Washington and Tashkent are continuing to work on other projects that Henick hopes will be ready in time for Mirziyoev’s planned trip to the United States to attend the G20 summit in Florida as an official observer.

Another issue on the bilateral agenda is the Jackson-Vanik amendment, a Cold War-era US trade provision that continues to apply to Uzbekistan and several other countries.

Henick said the provisions were routinely waived and did not significantly affect the embassy’s day-to-day work, but acknowledged their symbolic importance to the countries still covered by the measure.

President Trump and Rubio have made clear that they support lifting Jackson-Vanik, Henick said. He also pointed to a recent visit by US Representative Jason Smith, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, who met with Mirziyoev and committed to working in Congress toward lifting the restrictions.

For Coffey, however, the ultimate measure of success will be a measurable increase in private-sector investment flowing into Central Asia.

Such growth will take time, he said, but the Samarkand meetings may have planted the seeds for it.

Coffey also called for tangible progress on the Trans-Caspian trade route, including infrastructure projects and investment in oil and gas pipelines connecting the two shores of the Caspian Sea.

He suggested Washington could broaden its regional engagement beyond the five Central Asian states by considering a C6 format that includes Azerbaijan and deepening ties with the Organization of Turkic States.

The push for more American investment also raises questions about how Washington will ensure that new commercial relationships do not expose US companies to sanctioned actors, corruption, and other violations.

Some Central Asian countries have been identified as channels through which Russia has obtained goods subject to Western sanctions, making enforcement a particularly sensitive issue as the United States pursues closer economic ties.

Coffey said addressing sanctions evasion would require coordinated action by the Departments of Commerce, Treasury, and State, as well as the White House.

All available tools, he said, should be used to close loopholes and ensure investments comply with US interests, objectives, and laws.

Howard likewise warned that the success of new deals would depend on their terms and implementation, rather than simply the announcement of headline figures.

Investments must be structured to guard against exposure to sanctioned entities, corruption, and human rights violations, she said. That requires effective oversight, rigorous due diligence, and screening for connections to US adversaries.

Alex Raufoglu is RFE/RL's senior correspondent in Washington, D.C.

https://www.defensenews.com/news/pentago.heading: Groups seek clarity on motive behind Pentagon’s study of women in combat
https://www.defensenews.com/news/pentago.body:
A group of civil rights organizations sued the Defense Department for records behind its decision to study women’s “effectiveness” in combat roles a decade after the military opened those positions to women.

The lawsuit, filed by the American Civil Liberties Union, or ACLU, alongside two other groups, asks a federal court to enforce their request for information about why the Pentagon commissioned the study.

In a statement, Gillian Thomas, senior counsel for the ACLU’s Women’s Rights Project, argued that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has “repeatedly, without evidence, questioned women’s ability to serve in ground combat,” aims to deliver research to validate his “biased” views.

“Now, without explanation, he has commissioned a study of women’s performance and assigned it to a researcher with a record of criticizing women’s combat readiness,” she said. “The public has a right to know why, and what he plans to do with the results.”

In January, the Defense Department commissioned a non-profit research group called the Institute for Defense Analyses, which is largely funded by the federal government, to study the topic for six months.

However, according to the lawsuit, the study was reassigned to the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, or JHU/APL, in April 2026, where the lead researcher, Jane Pinelis, authored a 2015 study for the Marine Corps that found “negative effects of mixed-gender units.”

The lawsuit adds that the 2015 study “was widely criticized for its flawed design and biased analysis.” Those critics, including the Navy Secretary at the time, described it as attempting to show that men are stronger than women rather than establish minimum standards and see who could meet them.

Additionally, The War Horse reported that Hegseth relied heavily on that study to support his argument that women shouldn’t serve in combat roles in his book The War on Warriors.

“Dads push us to take risks. Moms put the training wheels on our bikes,” he wrote in the book. “We need moms. But not in the military, especially in combat units.”

In a November 2024 interview on the Sean Ryan Podcast, Hegseth shared his explicit view on the issue: “I’m straight up just saying we should not have women in combat roles.”

Although he has since softened his rhetoric on women in combat, critics say he continues to push the agenda under the guise of military standards.

According to the lawsuit, the ACLU, the National Women’s Law Center and the Service Women’s Action Network want Defense Department records showing the scope, purpose, methodology and anticipated use of the study.

Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

US President Donald Trump has accused Ukraine of giving nothing in return for US support.

"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us. Remember that," Trump told reporters in Washington on Monday.

Meanwhile, US news website Axios reported that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had complained about Washington withholding weapons deliveries.

Zelensky reportedly raised the accusation during a virtual meeting with US senators from both parties.

According to Zelensky, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was refusing to approve deliveries of Patriot and other air defence missiles, even though NATO countries had already paid for them, Axios reported, citing a transcript of the meeting.

"All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us," Zelensky was quoted as saying.

The Washington Post, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that the suspension also affected deliveries from other Ukrainian partners that required Washington's approval.

A senior US Defense Department official disputed the reports, telling dpa that there had been no changes to the programme under which NATO countries purchase US weapons for Ukraine. The same applied to intelligence-sharing, the official said.

Trump also stepped up his criticism of Kiev after Zelensky suggested that the US president's Kremlin-friendly approach put him on the wrong side of history.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump responded.

The Ukrainian president was "not helping matters much" in efforts to end the war, Trump said.

Vice President JD Vance on Monday declined to say whether he endorses Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection, after President Donald Trump recently threw his support behind the Israeli prime minister.

“I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterm,” Vance said in an interview with journalist Mark Halperin aboard Air Force Two. “I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections.”

Yet, Vance traveled to Budapest, Hungary, earlier this year to support Trump-endorsed Victor Orbán ahead of his election, which the longtime prime minister lost.

Vance said he wasn’t for or against endorsing Netanyahu.

“I’m not anti-endorsing him. I’m not pro-endorsing him. I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

Nine days before Israeli elections, Trump finally endorses Netanyahu

Trump had also previously held off endorsing Netanyahu.

“I’m not involved in [Israeli] politics anymore,” Trump told Time earlier this month.

But Trump gave his full-throated endorsement Saturday for Netanyahu, calling him a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” in a post on social media.

Vance’s apparent break from Trump in declining to endorse the prime minister comes just days before Israel’s election and as US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth traveled to Israel in an unannounced trip, according to two sources familiar and a US official.

Hegseth met Monday evening with Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, according to an Israeli source familiar with the details and another source familiar.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.heading: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan | US immigration | The Guardian
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.body:
More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday.

Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.

The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.

The decision marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.

Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a non-profit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the US, described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches”.

It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for US to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.

Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington thinktank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said.

“It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them.”

The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorians whose TPS was set to expire on 9 September. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the US.

Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.

Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when the DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.

The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive US administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.

Monday’s decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.

https://www.aa.com.tr/en/americas/trump-.body:
US President Donald Trump said Monday that it may be time for someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to negotiate on Kyiv's behalf.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about. Zelensky is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago," Trump told reporters before departing the White House.

"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine because what's happened? A tremendous number of people are dead. They're losing their male population," he said.

"Maybe it's time for Zelensky to get somebody else to negotiate," Trump added.

"Zelensky is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it, but I want to see people not die."

"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing," he added.

Asked whether he had agreed to a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Ukraine, Trump said he had not but was open to such talks.

"No, but I would do it. Not so much for Ukraine because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," he said.

Trump indicated that nuclear disarmament would be a priority in any such meeting.

"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," he said.

"We have more nuclear weapons than anybody. Russia is second, China is third, but catching up. China was way behind, and now they're catching up. It'll take about probably five years," Trump added.

Asked whether he would meet Putin and Xi to discuss ending the war without Zelenskyy present, Trump said he would do "anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not."

Trump also said Russia and China had provided limited support to Iran despite their close relations with Tehran.

"Russia could have done a lot more to help Iran. Russia's done very little for Iran. China could have done a lot more for Iran," he said.

"I view that as being a very positive thing," Trump added.

https://edition.cnn.com/2026/10/19/europ.heading: US-Ukraine relationship worsens amid Trump and Zelensky’s mutual distrust | CNN
https://edition.cnn.com/2026/10/19/europ.body:
The relationship between Ukraine and the United States is facing increasing strain over intelligence sharing, sanctions, Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy and the path to peace.

There also appears to be deepening mutual distrust between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky.

Trump on Monday accused Zelensky of not knowing what he was talking about and suggested it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”

Over the weekend Kyiv launched one of its biggest drone attacks this year on Russia, hitting a key oil terminal, in defiance of Trump’s demand that Ukraine stop hitting Russian refining plants.

The White House is trying to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices in the US ahead of crucial midterm elections, as diesel prices are at a record high.

Last week Trump called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace” and said Zelensky was more difficult to deal with than Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

In an interview on Sunday, Zelensky hit back, saying it was “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face,” an apparent reference to Trump’s relationship to Russia.

Trump again criticized Zelensky on Sunday, claiming in a Truth Social post that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

The relationship now seems to be at its lowest ebb since the explosive meeting at the White House 18 months ago.

Zelensky has consistently said he is open to peace negotiations if Ukraine’s security can be guaranteed.

The Ukrainian president said he spoke to US envoy, Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Sunday as part of “nonstop communication” to work towards the goal of peace. Zelensky added later he was hoping to meet the two “maybe in Norway in the coming days.” CNN has reached out to the White House for comment on the meeting.

“We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer,” Zelensky posted on X.

“Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end,” Zelensky added on Monday.

Zelensky also spoke to Pope Leo XIV on Monday, according to the Vatican.

The pope spoke to the Ukrainian president just days after a phone call with Putin in which he expressed his concern about the “grave humanitarian situation” in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where Ukrainian authorities say around 2,000 civilians are stuck without access to food or basic medicine.

Trump has defended recent concessions to Russia on sanctions, which have included a waiver to allow Russian diesel exports and another exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress.

“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote in his Sunday post.

In an interview Sunday with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Zelensky said the waivers strengthened Putin’s war against Ukraine while Moscow was failing on the battlefield.

There is growing anxiety in Kyiv and Europe that the Trump administration will make further concessions to Moscow in an effort to get Putin to agree to a peace deal.

Zelensky told “Meet the Press” that the US siding with Russia would be a “historic mistake.” He said he wanted to trust Trump and hoped he would change his attitude to Putin.

Asked if Trump was an ally of Ukraine, Zelensky said: “I hope so.”

On Monday, Zelensky appealed directly to the US Congress, holding an online meeting with a group of lawmakers from both parties. He described the current situation as “the most difficult situation from the very beginning of this war” and saying that it appears as if “some political decision has been made to slow down support for us.”

Ukraine is also perturbed by reports of a possible three-way meeting involving the US and China next month on settling the conflict – without Ukrainian involvement.

“I think there’s been talk of a meeting. I don’t know if anything’s been finalized,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said during a visit to Uzbekistan Monday.

Trump said on Monday that he’d consider a trilateral meeting with Putin and the Chinese leader Xi Jinping — but said that the sitdown would focus on denuclearization, not Russia’s war with Ukraine.

But Ukraine criticized the idea, arguing such a meeting would not help peace but “would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Monday.

“Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandizement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” Sybiha wrote on X.

The Kremlin said Monday that “no concrete proposals or agreements – neither regarding the meeting itself nor its potential agenda and content – have been discussed or put forward by anyone.”

Defying Trump’s demands, Ukraine is keeping up long-range strikes into Russia. One target at the weekend was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal. The terminal can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year. Ukraine’s Fire Point company, which makes the drones used in the attack, said there was a fire on the terminal’s grounds following the strike.

A logistics center in St. Petersburg was also attacked, according to Ozon, a Russian distribution company, as well as a data center for the Russian VKontakte social media platform.

One person was killed and five wounded in the attacks, with residential homes damaged as well, according to local authorities.

A week ago, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.

Neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such an agreement. Ukraine briefly halted such attacks, but Russia never stopped pounding Ukraine’s energy plants and cities.

“Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ​ago, Russia has ​deliberately ‌attacked ​Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors ⁠76 times,” Zelensky ​wrote on X Sunday.

On Monday, Zelensky said a Russian drone attack in the Kharkiv region killed six people, including three children. Sharing a blurred photograph of one of the victims – a small child in a stroller – Zelensky said the horrific image showed “the truth about this war.”

“Lives must be protected. Ukraine needs air defense. You can’t think about making money with Russia as long as it continues its asinine war,” he said on X.

Accusations have also flown over the cuts in US satellite intelligence provided to the Ukrainian military.

Zelensky repeated on Sunday that changes in the Starlink system owned by billionaire Elon Musk was limiting the speed of its short-range and battlefield drones, describing it as a “message from the American government.”

Musk said last week that the systems are owned and controlled by the US government, meaning that only the government could decide to place limits on their speed or usage.

The Trump administration has denied it ordered the service restricted. On Monday, Trump said he didn’t know who it was that restricted it, but would “like to find out.”

Similarly the Trump administration has pushed back on accusations from Kyiv that intelligence on incoming ballistic missiles is not being shared.

Zelensky said on Monday that Kyiv had received no advance warning of ballistic missile attacks on Sunday night – something he claims has occurred multiple times in the past week.

“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners.”

US satellite networks are critical in providing the Ukrainian military with warnings of incoming missiles. Russian ballistic missile attacks are aimed at crippling civilian life and destroying essential infrastructure.

“I don’t know where he’s getting these things or why he’s saying these things to the press,” Rubio told ‌reporters Monday. “You should go back and ask him. There’s been no pause.”

“What he should be focused on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That’s what he should be focused ​on,” Rubio said of Zelensky.

Kyiv and Washington see very different paths to that goal.

CNN’s Daria Tarasova, Anna Chernova, Julia Benbrook, Jennifer Hansler, Christopher Lamb, Kristen Holmes and Ivana Kottasová contributed to this report.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/ukra.heading: Ukraine needs another €70 billion, but where will the EU find the money? | Euronews
https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/ukra.body:
The European Union is scrambling to find an additional €70 billion for Ukraine next year, after Russia's escalating assault on the country and its economy rendered the bloc's existing financial support plans insufficient.

At the end of a two-day summit last week, EU leaders heard directly from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the scale of the shortfall.

"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you: for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," he said.

According to Zelenskyy, the extra injection of cash will help Ukraine ramp up domestic production of its cutting-edge drones to stop Russia's advances on the battlefield, disrupt its supply chains and undercut its war apparatus.

"We really need at least €70 billion additionally for next year," he added.

The appeal struck a chord. EU leaders tasked the European Commission with exploring ways to plug the gap, which is considerably larger than Brussels had anticipated.

Until now, the bloc based its support on the €90 billion loan that leaders signed off last December. The loan was designed to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's financial and military needs for 2026 and 2027 combined, with other allies covering the remaining third.

Crucially, the Commission devised the loan assuming that the war would end sometime in 2026. Instead, Moscow has intensified its offensive, including daytime attacks aimed at crippling Ukraine's already fragile economy.

Kyiv has spent weeks warning that it will need an additional $32.6 billion to support its budget and $45 billion for its armed forces next year – a combined $78 billion, or approximately €70 billion.

Brussels initially declined to comment on the staggering figure. But after several rounds of technical discussions, it has accepted the estimate and concluded that the money must be found if Ukraine is to sustain its war effort.

The €70 billion would come on top of the €45 billion the EU plans to disburse under its existing loan, as well as several billion euros from other programmes.

Faced with a swelling bill, Brussels has been quick to stress that the €70 billion will be a "joint effort" with other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada and Japan.

"We always said that we cannot walk this alone. We cannot do this all alone. Therefore, our partners in general must step up," a Commission spokesperson said.

"They have to come forward with pledges, and they have to deliver on those commitments. This is very important."

It is not yet clear how much of the €70 billion the EU will provide, given that the previous split of two-thirds vs one-third has not worked out as planned. Nor is it clear how quickly Kyiv will need the money. What is clear is that the options for raising such a vast sum at short notice are severely limited.

Adding to the pressure, the high-stakes negotiations will unfold in parallel with the bitter fight over the next long-term budget and the lead-up to the French presidential election, where frontrunner Marine Le Pen has vowed to end all aid to Ukraine.

Raising fresh joint EU debt on the financial markets, as Brussels is already doing for the €90 billion loan, currently appears the most likely option, according to diplomats and officials. The Commission could increase the existing credit facility, effectively extending the current financing arrangement.

The bloc, with its stable AAA credit rating, has become an in-demand bond issuer since the COVID-19 pandemic, with its auctions often oversubscribed. Mario Draghi, the former Italian Prime Minister and ECB President, has called for large-scale borrowing.

The financial landscape, however, has sharply deteriorated since December, when leaders signed off on the loan. Borrowing costs have soared worldwide in response to surging oil prices, rising public debt and strong demand for AI spending.

European countries have been hit particularly hard, especially those already heavily indebted. Belgium is now borrowing at rates comparable to Greece, while France is paying more than Italy.

This makes the prospect of fresh debt politically sensitive, even difficult, as it would add to the mounting pile of interest payments.

Yield on the bloc's 10-year bond has risen from 2.8% in January to 3.44% in September – a significant increase, although less pronounced than in many other markets.

"This is a dynamic that affects all insurers around the world, and our relative position importantly has not deteriorated," the Commission spokesperson said.

"We remain an extremely competitive issuer."

If joint borrowing emerges as the main option, several countries are expected to opt out.

Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic are already exempted from the €90 billion loan. At last week's summit, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said he and his Hungarian counterpart, Péter Magyar, had agreed to maintain the policy.

"If they (other countries) want to provide a loan to Ukraine, they can do so, but at least two countries are indicating at this point that we will not participate in this financial mechanism," Fico said. "We show solidarity in other ways."

Another country likely to sit it out is Bulgaria, whose new prime minister, Rumen Radev, has repeatedly criticised the bloc's military assistance to Ukraine.

In recent weeks, several countries have floated an alternative avenue to equip Ukraine with long-lasting financial firepower: the immobilised assets of the Russian Central Bank, worth a massive €210 billion across the bloc's territory.

Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland revived the debate in August. The Nordics, the Baltics, Germany and Ireland have since expressed support.

These are the same countries that last year pushed the hardest to channel the assets into a zero-interest credit for Ukraine. For the most part, they are the largest bilateral donors to Ukraine and see the assets as a way to ensure genuine burden-sharing.

The project failed when it bumped into Belgium's fierce resistance, which holds €185 billion of these assets in Euroclear, a depository in central Brussels.

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever warned that using the assets would amount to confiscation and have catastrophic consequences for the country. He demanded the total mutualisation of risks and uncapped guarantees against all possible liabilities.

Leaders recoiled at the prospect of bailing out Belgium's banking system and, at the last minute, opted for joint debt to set up the €90 billion loan.

Despite that setback, supporters of using the Russian assets have not abandoned the idea. Ukraine has consistently brought the topic into the conversation.

Zelenskyy said that if Europe does not use them, Russia would seek to retrieve them. (The US has reportedly pitched a plan to partially release the assets as an incentive for Russia to engage in the peace talks, but Europeans shot it down.)

"The main priority is that Russia doesn't have the opportunity to influence later on the discussion on these assets, because we know very clearly they want to bring these assets back," Zelenskyy said last week. "It's one of Russia's aims."

De Wever remains firmly opposed. During the summit, the Belgian premier, on his own initiative, took the floor to tell his peers that his objections remained unchanged, Euronews understands. He argued the money should be kept firmly locked in until the end of the war to prevent external meddling by Moscow or Washington.

The message was received. Officials and diplomats left the summit with the impression that the assets had little chance of succeeding this time around.

The failure of last year's proposal remains fresh in their minds. France and Italy, whose support would be crucial, are still considered reluctant to use the assets.

Belgium's position is even more entrenched. It opposes not only tapping the sovereign funds but also transferring them from Euroclear to an EU-owned custodian, a legal workaround that some have promoted to break the impasse.

"The issue will be coming up over and over. Eventually it may find a resolution. I don't think short-term it's going to be on the agenda, like this month or the next one," Katarína Mathernová, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, told Euronews.

"While the assets remain frozen and they are in Europe and under our regime and now under European jurisdiction, they certainly are for the leaders to discuss in the future. And I think that will happen, but not in the short term."

https://www.lrt.lt/en/news-in-english/19.heading: EU proposal for security protocol modelled on NATO’s Article 4 draws scepticism - LRT
https://www.lrt.lt/en/news-in-english/19.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed creating a European Union security protocol modelled on NATO’s Article 4 to coordinate responses to hybrid attacks, but the idea has so far received limited support and raised concerns about duplication and political divisions within the bloc.

Von der Leyen raised the proposal amid a series of suspected hybrid threats across Europe, including drone incursions in several EU countries and an attempted attack at Leipzig airport. On the eve of her annual address, a drone was shot down over Lithuania.

“I believe the time has come for a European Article 4 – an emergency security protocol. If one member state activates it, all the others would come together,” von der Leyen said.

NATO’s Article 4 provides for consultations among allies when a member believes its security, territorial integrity or political independence is threatened. It has been invoked nine times.

EU defence ministers have discussed von der Leyen’s proposal, but support appears limited.

“The Commission president has raised the idea, and now we have to work on it,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.

Military officials say they will follow the political decisions made by EU leaders, while warning against unnecessary duplication of existing security arrangements.

“The vast majority of EU countries are also NATO members. I think we should avoid duplication here,” Lithuanian army commander Gen. Raimundas Vaikšnoras said. “We need to find the right balance so that we do not interfere with or overshadow one another.”

Experts are also divided over whether the EU needs a separate protocol.

Marija Martišiūtė, an analyst at the European Policy Centre, said such a mechanism could be useful because NATO allies are not always willing to invoke Article 4. An EU protocol would give a country facing an attack another avenue to seek support, she said.

Under the proposed mechanism, a member state could present its assessment of an incident, explain how it occurred and identify the perceived threat before seeking assistance or a joint decision from other EU members.

The protocol could also provide for potential responses, Martišiūtė said, including an operation, increased monitoring and vigilance, sanctions or financial measures.

But Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an analyst at the Bruegel think tank, called the proposal a mistake.

“It is a terrible idea. It just diverts attention,” he said.

Kirkegaard argued that NATO’s Article 4 consultations can already risk becoming a forum for empty talk when 32 allies cannot agree on a response. An EU version would be even more difficult, he said, given differences among member states over defence policy and spending.

He pointed to four neutral EU countries and said some members, including Ireland and Malta, were reluctant to engage on defence issues. Austria, he added, was also hesitant to some extent.

The EU already has a treaty provision requiring member states to provide aid and assistance if another member is the victim of armed aggression on its territory. Earlier this year, EU leaders asked the European Commission to draw up an action plan for implementing that mutual-assistance clause.

So far, member states have held tabletop exercises to exchange ideas about what such assistance would mean in practice. It remains unclear when the Commission will present a concrete action plan.

https://www.rfi.fr/en/international-news.heading: EU unveils strategy to boost Arctic presence
https://www.rfi.fr/en/international-news.body:
Brussels (Belgium) (AFP) – The EU is to unveil plans to bolster its foothold in the Arctic Tuesday, as it grapples with pressure from Russia and the United States in the key strategic region.

From critical raw materials to icebreakers and undersea cables, the bloc wants to up its presence in the geopolitical battleground, according to a draft of its new "strategy for the Arctic" seen by AFP.

"The new reality in the Arctic requires Europe to be a strong and reliable partner. That is precisely what we aim to achieve with our new strategy," said Jozef Sikela, the EU's head of international partnerships.

"It addresses the region's most pressing challenges, from accelerating climate change to growing security and geopolitical tensions, and sets out how Europe should respond."

Competition is on the rise in the Arctic as global warming causes sea ice to melt. Countries such as Russia, China and the United States have been ramping up activity, racing to claim natural resources and new maritime routes.

With three Arctic nations among its 27 members -- Denmark, Finland and Sweden -- the European Union has skin in the game.

And President Donald Trump's repeated threats to bring Greenland -- a vast, autonomous Danish territory -- under US control have rattled Europe.

Given that what happens in the far north also has repercussions further south, the strategy, which is to be presented by the EU chief Ursula von der Leyen, aims to set out a common EU approach to the region.

The draft seen by AFP stresses the need to cooperation with "like-minded" non-EU nations, such as Canada, Britain and Norway, and envisages a regular summit of "Northern Neighbourhood" partners.

Only recently a key ally in the region, the United States is listed among those who could participate, but the country is otherwise more noticeable for its absence from the remainder of the document.

While Trump's tone has cooled since the beginning of the year, eventually leading to the signing of a security deal with Greenland and Denmark, many in Europe remain wary.

The United States is named only a handful of times in the 20-page paper, compared with almost two dozen mentions for Canada.

Some of the initiatives listed in the strategy seemingly aim to cut dependencies on Washington.

According to the draft, Brussels is planning a "sovereign and secure" submarine cable to connect Greenland with the EU's mainland as part of a broader "Pan-Arctic" cable project also linking Canada, Japan and South Korea.

The bloc is also working to provide satellite connectivity in the Arctic through satellite constellation project IRIS², which aims to rival Elon Musk's Starlink.

How to counter an aggressive Russia is also top of mind, with the document pointing to hybrid threats such as "drone incursions" and the sabotage of undersea cables.

The strategy envisages better data-sharing to monitor Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of sanctions-busting oil tankers.

And it stresses the importance of boosting Europe's icebreaker fleet, saying Brussels will develop options for joint procurement, pooling and sharing of polar vessels with allies.

Investments in renewable energy and critical raw material projects are also foreseen, among a series of other plans.

https://www.catalannews.com/politics/ite.heading: Andorra signs EU association deal to access single market while keeping border controls
https://www.catalannews.com/politics/ite.body:
Andorra has formally signed an association agreement with the European Union that would give the Catalan-speaking principality access to the EU single market while allowing it to retain border controls and remain outside the bloc.

The deal provides for the free movement of goods, people, services and capital, although Andorra will not join the EU or the Schengen area.

A separate arrangement will preserve the absence of border checks with France and Spain.

Andorran Prime Minister Xavier Espot described small countries as "reliable, constructive and committed partners" in Europe, despite their "different" histories.

The agreement, signed on Monday, follows a negotiation process launched in December 2014.

It still requires European Parliament consent, followed by a consultative referendum in Andorra, expected after the parliament votes, potentially in January.

If voters back the deal, Andorra's parliament must approve it by a two-thirds majority before final ratification by the Council of the European Union.

The agreement also requires the consent of Andorra's co-princes, French President Emmanuel Macron and the Bishop of Urgell, Catalonia, Josep-Lluís Serrano Pentinat.

The deal includes transitional periods for sensitive sectors, including 30 years for tobacco, 15 years for financial services and seven years for telecommunications.

Mobile roaming charges are expected to be abolished after seven years, subject to minimum quality and coverage requirements.

Andorrans would gain the right to live, work, study, retire and establish businesses in EU countries under the same conditions as EU nationals.

However, they would not be able to vote in European elections, and Andorra would not be required to contribute to the EU budget.

An economic study cited by the Andorran government estimates the agreement could increase the Pyrenean microstate's GDP by 5% by 2050 under the most conservative scenario.

NEW YORK, 20 October 2026 — The UN Security Council meets on Tuesday to discuss Kosovo, with a new report warning of political deadlock and little progress in talks with Serbia.

The report says security remains broadly stable but tensions persist in northern Kosovo, while agreements reached through EU-mediated talks remain largely unfulfilled.

It also raises concerns over accountability for the deadly 2023 Banjska attack and the fate of 1,579 people still missing since the Kosovo war.

UN mission chief Peter Due will present the report, which covers March to September.

The meeting comes amid disagreements over the UN mission's future. Washington wants it closed, while Russia and China oppose reducing its presence.

"A series of NATO experiments and trials of new defence technologies has begun in Latvia this week. Parallel activities are taking place in three directions, namely experiments and technological tests in the latest generation of communications solutions, or the Digital Backbone Experiment (DiBaX 2026), the direction of development of anti-drone capabilities, which includes sensor and effector tests (LCI-X, Layered Counter UAS Initiative), and tests for the development of deep strike capabilities (NGT, Next Generation Targeting)," the Ministry revealed.

The experiments are taking place both at the major Ādaži military base near Rīga and the recently-created Sēlija military ranges on a considerably larger scale than ever before.

"The aim of "DiBaX 2026" is to test digital infrastructure in conjunction with various defence technologies to ensure effective and coordinated technology operation in NATO operations. This year, the programme has been expanded to focus on the integration of sensors and effectors, with a particular emphasis on sensor capabilities needed to detect, identify and respond to emerging threats," the Ministry said.

Activities in 2026 include "experimental field tests, network infrastructure trials, and integrated scenarios involving sensors, communication and unmanned systems, decision support tools, and capabilities for defense against unmanned aircraft."

Nearly 100 defence industry companies from more than 20 countries are participating in the experiments, along with representatives of the armed forces of allied countries.

"The DiBaX experiment in Latvia, which has been running for the fifth year in a row, demonstrates our ability to host and provide an environment for testing and improving the latest defense technologies in various conditions. This experience allows us not only to test innovative digital solutions in an environment close to realistic operational conditions, but also to strengthen cooperation with NATO allies and promote technology interoperability," said Minister of Defense Raivis Melnis.

"DiBaX 2026" is led by NATO's Allied Command Transformations (ACT) in cooperation with the Latvian Ministry of Defence, the National Armed Forces and LMT Defence.

The experiment will conclude at the end of October with the event "NATO FUSE", the aim of which is to practically test and improve new technological solutions, involving both military representatives and the defence industry.
